title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI

content:
Training on long documents across several GPUs creates more than a compute problem. Each GPU also needs the right attention mask: the rules that determine which tokens may attend to which other tokens. If those rules leave one GPU with more work than the others, the entire training step waits for it.
FlashMask-3 starts with how masks are stored, then uses that representation to select work, distribute it, and overlap communication with computation. The paper reports a 7.3–11.0% improvement in full training throughput for a MoE model with a 128K context on 128 H100 GPUs. That result must be distinguished from the speedup of the attention kernel alone (§4.3, Table 1).
Paper · Code Splitting a long sequence also creates a mask problemAttention computes how much information each token takes from other tokens. A mask rules out relationships that are not allowed. For example, when several documents are packed into one input, tokens from different documents can be prevented from attending to each other. Sliding-window attention, which only allows nearby tokens, is another example.
Representing a mask as a large table becomes expensive. With $n$ tokens there are $n^2$ token pairs, so storing and processing the mask grows costly as the input gets longer. The earlier FlashMask reduces storage to $O(n)$ by representing structured masks with interval boundaries (§2.2).
Using several GPUs adds another challenge. Context Parallelism (CP) distributes attention work for a long sequence across GPUs. Each GPU needs a mask for its assigned tokens, and equal token counts do not imply equal amounts of computation. Simply splitting the sequence into equally sized pieces does not guarantee balanced work (§2.3).
FlashMask-3 connects these two problems. It aims to use compressed masks efficiently inside a GPU kernel while preventing mask processing and communication from becoming bottlenecks when work is distributed across GPUs.
Store boundaries instead of a large tableIn an attention matrix, rows correspond to queries, the tokens requesting information, and columns to keys, the tokens being attended to. FlashMask stores the query intervals that are masked out for each key. For masks that fit this representation, each key requires at most two masked intervals, or four boundary values (§2.2).
A small example shows why this helps construct per-GPU masks. This is an illustrative example, not a measurement from the paper.
Suppose eight tokens are split across two GPUs, and the masked query interval for one key is $[6,8)$ in global coordinates. GPU A handles queries 0–3, while GPU B handles queries 4–7.
GPU Assigned global query interval Overlap with masked interval GPU-local coordinates A $[0,4)$ None Empty interval B $[4,8)$ $[6,8)$ $[2,4)$ GPU B only needs to subtract its starting offset, 4. GPU A clips the out-of-range boundaries to the end of its range, obtaining an empty interval. If both already know the global boundaries and their own assignments, they need no communication to perform this conversion.
The paper extends this idea to cases where one GPU owns several noncontiguous chunks. It clips boundaries to the assigned chunks, shifts them into local coordinates, and merges them with a maximum operation. Theorem 1 establishes that this conversion preserves the original masking relationships (§3.2, Appendix C.1).
Here, zero communication refers only to converting mask boundaries into local coordinates. GPUs still need to exchange key and value data for attention computation.
Reuse the boundaries to choose and distribute workCompact mask storage alone does not make a GPU fast. FlashMask-3 uses the same boundaries to skip unnecessary work and distribute the remaining work more evenly.
Filter blocks before computing themThe GPU kernel processes the attention matrix in small blocks. If an entire block is masked, it needs neither a data load nor a matrix multiplication. A partially masked block still needs computation with masking applied.
FlashMask-3’s KV Index Generator identifies these cases and produces a list of blocks to compute. The loader fetches blocks from that list, while the matrix-multiplication threads concentrate on computation. This separates mask inspection from the main compute path while using Hopper’s asynchronous data transfers (TMA) and matrix-multiplication instructions (WGMMA) (§3.1).
A simple porting experiment illustrates why this separation matters. For a 128K Document mask, forward throughput was 19.0 TFLOPs/s for a FA3-style Hopper port without the KV Index Generator, versus 577.6 TFLOPs/s for the complete FlashMask-3 implementation. The full implementation includes other optimizations, however, so the entire difference cannot be attributed to this component alone (Appendix D.4, Table 7).
Balance actual computation rather than token countsTwo equally long chunks can require different amounts of work if one has more masked blocks. FlashMask-3’s HCC-IPO algorithm accounts for that difference. It first balances computation across GPUs, adjusts assignments to reduce cross-node transfers, then rebalances within each node (§3.3).
A similar imbalance can occur inside one GPU: some execution units finish early while others remain occupied. The PPT scheduler lets a GPU thread block take another task when it finishes its current one. These two scheduling mechanisms reduce waiting across GPUs and within each GPU, respectively (§3.1).
Overlap necessary communication with computationEven with context parallelism, each GPU needs key and value data held by other GPUs. FlashMask-3 skips transfers of chunks that the mask makes entirely unnecessary and separates inter-node and intra-node communication routes. During backward computation, it divides work into segments so that communication for one segment overlaps computation for the next (§3.4).
Overall pipelineSaying “the mask is a bottleneck” combines three operations: building a large table of masked entries, selecting blocks to compute, and assigning work to GPUs. Slow preparation or uneven assignments can delay the next training step.
The figure uses small illustrative examples to make those operations visible. Its three panels are independent examples, not performance measurements from the paper.
In the first panel, green entries are token pairs to compute; gray entries can be skipped. For key 6, rows 0–3 are masked, which can be recorded as the interval [0, 4). The kernel uses such boundaries to avoid loading or computing fully masked blocks (§2.2, §3.1).
The second panel converts boundaries into GPU-local coordinates. Global interval [6, 8) becomes [2, 4) on GPU B. This conversion needs no communication between GPUs, but attention still requires key and value data transfers (§3.2).
In the third panel, assigning the same number of tasks to each GPU produces costs of 14 and 6. Reassigning the tasks yields 10 each. The actual HCC-IPO also considers cross-node transfer costs. The change from 14 to 10 uses arbitrary illustrative work units, not measured speedups (§3.3).
Finally, necessary transfers overlap computation. For example, the system can fetch data for a subsequent segment while computing a ready segment, reducing waiting. The figure shows storage, coordinate conversion, and assignment; it does not depict the detailed communication-overlap implementation (§3.4).
How much faster is actual training?The most useful result to examine first is full training throughput. Faster attention can produce a smaller overall gain when other training operations remain unchanged.
The experiment trained a MoE model with 118B total and 14B active parameters at a 128K context length. It used 128 H100 GPUs, CP degree 16, and an 8K local sequence per GPU. The baseline below already uses the FlashMask-3 kernel, but retains Dual Chunk assignment and all-gather communication with the proposed balancing and overlap disabled. This table therefore measures the additional benefit of distributed execution optimizations, rather than simply replacing the attention kernel (§4.3, Table 1).
Mask sparsity Baseline throughput FlashMask-3 throughput Full training gain Attention forward+backward gain 70% 712.6 tokens/s/GPU 764.7 tokens/s/GPU 7.3% 24.5% 80% 753.3 tokens/s/GPU 811.4 tokens/s/GPU 7.7% 42.1% 86% 812.4 tokens/s/GPU 902.1 tokens/s/GPU 11.0% 44.9% The table reproduces the paper’s mean values. Standard deviations and component-level experiments are available in the collapsed source tables below.
The distinction between the final two columns matters. Attention computation improved by up to 44.9%, but full training throughput improved by up to 11.0%. Training also includes operations this method does not change, such as gradient synchronization and optimizer updates. Reading the result as “44.9% faster training” would misstate its scope.
In a separate distributed attention experiment, total forward+backward throughput was 1.09–1.46 times that of MagiAttention. That experiment kept the local sequence length at 8K per GPU while varying CP degree from 4 to 32. Its results should not be treated as the same metric as full training throughput above (§4.2, Table 5).
Does FlashMask-3 beat FlashAttention-3 on one GPU? Not for the five masks compared in Table 6: its throughput was 0.71–1.00 times FA3’s. Its value lies in supporting a broader range of structured masks alongside distributed execution, rather than winning every FA3 comparison (Appendix D.4).
Limitations to check before adoptionThe first question is whether the mask fits this representation. If the masked queries for a key cannot be expressed as two intervals, the current format cannot be used directly. The kernel also targets Hopper’s TMA and WGMMA facilities; matching these gains on another GPU requires implementation work and validation. Both are limitations acknowledged by the authors (Appendix A).
The communication optimizations also depend on hardware layout. They exploit fast intra-node NVLink and slower inter-node links, and hierarchical routing currently applies to forward all-gather. Other topologies and an extension to backward reduce-scatter need further validation (Appendix A, C.4).
From a reviewer’s perspective, assignment overhead deserves attention too. The paper precomputes scheduling decisions and prefetches them to hide their cost during execution. If masks change too often to reuse this preparation, the benefit may shrink. In Figure 7(b), IPO’s load-balance advantage over the simpler LPT is only about 0.01 where it improves the result. Whether that extra scheduling complexity is useful for a particular workload needs separate evaluation (§4.4, Appendix D.5).
The scope of quality validation also matters. The mask conversion preserves the original masking relationships, and the paper compares training losses across 1,581 steps. It does not provide a separate downstream benchmark evaluation (Theorem 1, Appendix D.3).
FlashMask-3 is worth examining when long documents, structured masks, and multi-GPU training on Hopper are all required. Its central contribution is to use mask boundaries as information for deciding actual computation and communication, beyond merely storing the mask compactly. An adoption assessment should check mask compatibility, GPU and network layout, then full training throughput.

title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention

content:
Paper From ‘Author’ to ‘Reviewer’ for the Strong Model: Trajectory-Level Speculative Execution in SpecAgentTL;DR — Instead of having a Strong model generate every step of a tool-using agent, a Weak model executes several steps first by calling real read tools and stops just before the first state change. The Strong model reads the entire draft in a single prefill and commits only the longest semantically valid prefix. On τ²-Bench, it maintains quality within 1 point of Strong-only while reducing HBM-read by 43–57% and wall time to 41–54%; on MCP-Atlas edge–cloud, it uses only 36–50% of Strong output tokens and recovers 53–75% of the quality gap (source: Abstract, Tab. 2, Tab. 3).
Numbers at a Glance Models: Weak Qwen3.5-4B (dense, 4B params), Strong Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (MoE, 397B total/17B active, 512 experts, top-10 active, vocabulary 248,320) (source: §4.1, Tab. 6). Training: No additional training. At inference time, the protocol, verifier prompt, and benchmark adapter are the entire method (source: §4.1, Appx. D). Serving: H20 GPU, Strong 16-way tensor parallelism, Weak 1 GPU, 8 tasks running concurrently, up to 100 steps (source: §4.1, Appx. A). Key results: On τ², HBM-read 43–57%, wall time 41–54%, Strong calls from 13.1–13.8 to 3.1. On MCP-Atlas, Strong output tokens 36–50%, API cost 59–81% (source: Tab. 2, Tab. 3). Not reported in the original: context window limit, TTFT/TPOT, KV-cache size, training compute, energy/PUE have no numbers in the paper. Per-task token counts (e.g., VitaBench 28.4k uncached tokens/task) are reported. 1. Background: Agent Cost Scales with the Number of StepsA tool-using agent produces a long trajectory of tool calls, not a single question-answer exchange. Table 1 presents representative trajectory lengths: 20–30 turns for MCP services, 30–80 turns for τ², 40–60 turns for AutomationBench, and 50–100 turns for VitaBench (source: Tab. 1). In existing designs, a single Strong model decodes all these steps token by token. Serving cost scales with trajectory length, and the bottleneck is the Strong model’s autoregressive decoding (source: §1).
Many steps are routine: order lookup, record reading, re-searching. A Weak model suffices for a substantial number of steps, yet the dominant design assigns every step to the Strong model. Prior work has tried to divide this work in roughly three ways.
Routers/cascades choose one model per query. The Strong model still generates every step of the selected query (source: §2). Collaborative agents decide which model acts at each step. But the model in control still generates each step from scratch (source: §2). Speculative agents have the Weak model draft the next action and the Strong model verify it. However, the draft is usually accepted only when it matches the Strong model’s own action, so the Strong model must still generate the reference step. The work is overlapped, not removed (source: §2). Recent step-level critics introduce loose matching instead of exact match, but they check only one step at a time and mainly handle search-style tasks where actions do not change the environment (source: §2). This makes the research gap clear.
Research gap — Can the Strong model be a reviewer of multiple steps rather than the generator of every step? That review must be grounded in real tool observations, occur only just before irreversible state changes, and preserve valid progress even when it differs from what the Strong model would have written (source: §1, §2, §3).
Within the scope the paper compares, the landscape at publication is as follows. Strong-only is the quality baseline at 86.0/88.6% on τ² Airline/Retail, 15.2% on AutomationBench, and 48.0% on VitaBench, but incurs large HBM-read and wall time. Weak-only is far cheaper with a 4B model but reaches only 6.8% on AutomationBench and 34.0% on VitaBench. AgentCollab is close to Strong on τ² at 85.3/85.7%, but its Strong calls are 18.5/16.6, more than Strong-only’s 13.8/13.1, and its wall time is longer as well. Speculative Actions targets latency and keeps the Strong model as the actor (source: Tab. 2, §2). In other words, the problem is finding a better operating point between “Strong quality” and “Weak cost.”
2. Core Hypothesis The authors hypothesize that by using SpecAgent, in which a weak model drafts multiple steps with real read tool calls and a strong model semantically validates the draft in a single prefill just before a state change, one can eliminate the Strong-only per-step autoregressive decoding and cut HBM traffic and wall time roughly in half while maintaining quality within 1 point on τ²-Bench.
This hypothesis decomposes into three premises. First, the draft must be grounded. The Weak model must choose the next step based on observations from real read tools, not imagined observations (source: §3.2). Second, execution must be safe. The first state-changing action is held rather than executed, and the environment is not changed before the Strong model’s review (source: §3.1, §3.2). Third, review must be cheap. Reading multiple steps in a single prefill must cost less than decoding those steps one by one, and semantic prefix acceptance must preserve the Weak model’s valid progress (source: §3.3).
Contributions by Type A new inference and serving protocol (not a new model architecture): trajectory-level draft–verify–repair at the read/write boundary, verification of multiple steps in a single prefill, and a fused replacement attempt for the first rejected step. The Strong model is a reviewer, not the author of each step (source: §3, Alg. 1, Fig. 1). A new analytical model: Propositions 1–2 predict Strong decode cost from acceptance rate, chunk length, verdict length, and repair probability (source: §3.3, Appx. C). A new application of an existing idea: moving speculative decoding’s draft–verify to the irreversible action boundary of tool-using agents (source: §2). There is no new dataset and no new model training. This improves reproducibility but also means performance depends heavily on off-the-shelf models and prompts.
The Authors’ Case for SuperiorityThe authors’ core argument is that SpecAgent “removes rather than overlaps” the Strong model’s work. In existing speculative agents, the Strong model keeps generating reference steps, so the gain stays limited to latency. SpecAgent has the Strong model read a long trajectory segment at once and decode only a short verdict (source: §1, §2). The second argument is semantic acceptance. Agent tasks have multiple valid paths, so steps that are valid for the goal should be preserved even if they do not exactly match what the Strong model would have written. In the ablation, switching to exact match drops Retail Pass@1 from 87.7% to 82.5% and increases FLOPs from 0.81 PFLOP to 1.37 PFLOP, a 70% rise (source: §3.2, Fig. 4). The third argument is the predictive power of the cost model. Strong traffic consumed by verification and repair matched predicted and observed HBM within 0.01 (source: §5, Tab. 4).
3. SpecAgent: How It Works3.1 Reads, Writes, and the Reversible BoundarySpecAgent views tool-use tasks as a partially observable Markov decision process. The environment has a hidden state $s$, such as a database or workspace, which the agent cannot see directly. At each step it emits an action $a_t$ (usually a tool call) and receives an observation $o_t$. The policy is conditioned on the task $u$ and the history
$$ H_t = \big(u,(a_1,o_1),\ldots,(a_t,o_t)\big) $$(source: §3.1). Two policies share the same interface: a cheap Weak model $\pi_W$ and a Strong model $\pi_S$ whose quality we want to preserve.
Actions fall into two classes. Reads return observations and do not change state, such as searches or lookups. State changes alter state, such as modifying a record or submitting a final result (source: §3.1). This distinction is the principle of the method. Errors left in the history can be erased and recovered from. Because a read did not change state, deleting it from the history leaves the environment as it was. In contrast, an error that reached the environment is not undone by fixing the history. A changed record does not revert, and a submitted result is not withdrawn (source: §3.1).
Speculation therefore proceeds freely while execution is reversible and verifies only at the boundary where errors become irreversible. Earlier verification wastes the Strong model on steps that can still be rolled back, and later verification is too late (source: §3.1). Note that “reversible” here means logical rollback. Deleting a rejected read from the history may still leave traces such as access logs in external services. What the paper guarantees is that “actions classified as state changes are not executed before review,” not that every physical effect of speculation is rolled back (source: Appx. D).
3.2 Three Beats: Draft, Verify, Repair Original Fig. 1 (PDF p.3). (a) Strong-only decodes every step token by token. (b) SpecAgent has the Weak model execute reads immediately and build a draft; when the first write is held, the Strong model reviews the entire draft in a single prefill. Bars indicate the Strong model’s relative memory reads.
On the left (a) of the figure, the Strong model autoregressively generates find user, get order, check policy, and refund order. On the right (b), the Weak model actually executes reads in steps 1–3 and leaves exchange item in step 4 held. The Strong model reads steps 1–4 in a single prefill, accepts through step 3, and replaces step 4 with refund order. The key is that the Strong model’s job shifts from “generating each step” to “one review plus a short repair” (source: Fig. 1, §3.2).
The concrete procedure is Algorithm 1 (source: Alg. 1).
Draft. From the current history $H_t$, the Weak model drafts a chunk of up to $K$ steps. Reads execute immediately; upon encountering the first state-changing action, it marks that action as $\perp$, appends it to the end of the chunk, and stops. Later steps depend on the outcome of that action and cannot be executed in advance. If all $K$ steps are filled with reads, the chunk is committed without review (source: §3.2). Verify. The Strong model reads $H_t$ and the chunk in a single prefill and returns $(j,r,\tilde a)$. $j$ is the length of the longest acceptable prefix, $r$ is the reason for the first rejection, and $\tilde a$ is an optional replacement action. Acceptance is semantic. It asks whether the step is a valid move toward the task, not whether it matches what the Strong model would have written (source: §3.2). Repair. If $j=n$, commit the read prefix $n-1$ and execute the held action. If $j\lt n$, commit only through prefix $j$; if $\tilde a$ passes tool-schema and executability checks, use it. Otherwise, the Strong model performs one repair turn with $H_t$ and $r$. Because repair is the Strong model’s own step, it is committed without further review. The rejected suffix, including the held action, is discarded, and the next draft starts only from the committed history (source: §3.2, Alg. 1). An important design point is that the verifier does not see the Weak model’s reasoning process. It sees only the committed actions and observations plus the draft’s actions and observations (source: Appx. D). Verification is therefore grounded in real observations, not “plausible explanations.” In addition, a fused replacement must be a single tool call, match the argument schema, and be actually executable. Otherwise, it falls back to a separate repair turn (source: §3.2, Appx. D).
Chunk size is $K=6$ on τ², VitaBench, and MCP-Atlas, and $K=8$ on AutomationBench (source: §4.1, Tab. 9). This value bounds how much reading accumulates before committing without review (source: Appx. D). Depending on the benchmark adapter, the final message may also be held. On AutomationBench and MCP-Atlas, the final message is the graded answer and is treated like a write, whereas on τ² and VitaBench replies are not held (source: Appx. D).
3.3 Illustrative Example: A Single Refund RequestThis is an illustrative example built along the flow of Fig. 1. The order ID, amount, and day counts below are hypothetical values for explanation, not paper numbers. They are not real τ² logs but a construction to show state changes at each step.
Task: “Please refund order A-1001.” Initial state: the order is delivered, not refunded, 12 days have passed since delivery, and the policy allows refunds within 30 days.
Step Weak model draft Class Executed? Environment state 1 find_user("minji") Read Executed user_id=U7 2 get_order(U7,"A-1001") Read Executed Delivered, 120 USD, 12 days ago 3 check_policy("refund", 12) Read Executed Within 30 days, refundable 4 exchange_item("A-1001") Write Held refunded=false The Weak model encounters the first state-changing action at step 4 and stops. The Strong model reads $H_t$ and steps 1–4 in a single prefill and returns accepted_steps=3, replacement_action=refund_order("A-1001"), and the reason “the user requested a refund and the order is within the 30-day policy.” Steps 1–3 are valid reads grounded in real observations. Step 4 is rejected because it misinterprets the user’s goal as an exchange. Because step 4 was not executed, the environment has not changed yet (source: Fig. 1, §3.2).
The meanings of the prefix branches are as follows.
$j=3$: commit steps 1–3 and replace step 4 with the Strong model’s replacement action. The example above is this case. $j=4$: commit steps 1–3 and execute held action 4 as is. This is the case where the Strong model considers all steps through 4 valid. $j=2$: commit only steps 1–2 and discard steps 3–4. Because step 3’s observation also disappears from the history, the Strong model repairs again from step 3. $j=0$: discard the entire chunk and have the Strong model write from the first step. In this example, semantic acceptance does not ask “did the Weak model read in exactly the same order as the Strong model?” For instance, even if the Weak model calls search_orders once more before get_order, that observation can remain in the prefix if it is valid and helps the goal. Conversely, if the policy was misread at step 3 or the order ID at step 4 is wrong, the prefix is cut at that point. This is the difference between exact match and semantic acceptance (source: §3.2).
3.4 Why Review Is Cheaper Than Generation: Prefill vs DecodeAutoregressive decoding performs one forward pass per token and reads the model’s active weights from HBM on each pass. When the batch is small, decode is bound by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic. Prefill processes multiple tokens with a single weight read, reducing weight traffic but increasing FLOPs because the matrix multiplies grow (source: §3.3, §5). SpecAgent’s cost model exploits this asymmetry.
Let $d$ be the weight pass of one step in Strong-only, $v$ the weight pass of a verdict, $n$ the chunk length, $p_u$ the average per-step acceptance rate for task $u$, and $\rho$ the probability that a separate repair turn is needed. Proposition 1 predicts the Strong model’s time and memory traffic per committed step relative to Strong-only as follows (source: Prop. 1, Appx. C).
$$ R_u = \frac{1-p_u}{1-p_u^n}\cdot\frac{v}{d} + \rho(1-p_u) $$The limits make the intuition clear. If $p_u=0$, then $R_u=v/d+\rho$, the cost of paying a verdict and a repair at every step. If $p_u\to 1$, then $R_u\to v/(nd)$, the cost of one verdict shared across $n$ steps. The gain grows with higher acceptance, longer chunks, shorter verdicts, and fewer separate repairs. Read-only chunks committed without review lower $R_u$ further (source: Prop. 1, §3.3).
Latency adds the Weak model’s drafting cost. Let $\kappa$ be the time of one Weak step relative to one Strong-only step; then the end-to-end time per committed step is (source: Prop. 2)
$$ L_u = R_u + \kappa\frac{n(1-p_u)}{1-p_u^n} $$The second term is the number of Weak steps that must be drafted to produce one committed step. As $p_u\to 1$, it approaches 1. SpecAgent is therefore faster than Strong-only only if one Weak step is sufficiently cheaper than one Strong step. This model ignores tool latency (source: Prop. 2). When this condition breaks in real deployments reappears in the MCP-Atlas results.
There is also a measurable form. Let $c_v$ be the number of verifications per committed step, $c_r$ the number of separate repairs, and $\bar v$, $\bar d_r$, $\bar d$ the average output tokens of a verdict, a repair, and a Strong-only step, respectively. Then the Strong traffic ratio is (source: §5)
$$ R = c_v\frac{\bar v}{\bar d} + c_r\frac{\bar d_r}{\bar d} $$Table 4 evaluates this expression on log token counts. On τ², the Strong model reviewed about once every 7 committed steps, and decoding tokens fell to 17–30% of Strong-only. Predicted HBM ratios matched observations within 0.01 on every benchmark. Generation time matched predictions on τ² and was lower than predicted on AutomationBench and VitaBench (source: §5, Tab. 4). This match is the empirical basis for the claim that “the savings come from decoding.”

On MCP-Atlas, SpecAgent sits between Weak-only and Strong-only for all three Strong models. Quality gap recovery is 53% for Qwen, 72% for GLM-5, and 75% for DeepSeek. Strong output tokens fall from 3.6k→1.8k (50%), 4.6k→2.1k (46%), and 10.6k→3.8k (36%), while API cost drops from 1.39→1.12 USD (81%), 8.91→5.54 USD (62%), and 1.37→0.81 USD (59%) (source: Tab. 3). HBM-read also falls in all three cases (source: Tab. 3). Because this 101-task subset is somewhat easier than the full benchmark, absolute scores cannot be compared directly with the public leaderboard (source: Appx. A). SpecAgent’s quality tracks the Strong model’s quality, because the Strong model is the one judging and repairing the draft (source: §5).
There is an important asymmetry here. The fraction of the quality gap recovered (53–75%) is larger than the fraction of Strong tokens used (36–50%). That is, one Strong token used inside SpecAgent buys more quality than one token used in Strong-only (source: §4.3). As Strong-only token counts grow from 3.6k to 4.6k to 10.6k tokens per task, SpecAgent’s token share falls from 50% to 46% to 36%, because the amortized verdict covers more steps (source: §5). Wall time, however, does not fall clearly. Qwen goes from 105 to 120 seconds, GLM-5 from 110 to 108 seconds, and DeepSeek from 151 to 215 seconds, showing little gain or even an increase (source: Tab. 3). Because the local Weak model spends about 109 seconds per task and the hosted Strong model spends 105–151 seconds, the latency term in Proposition 2 does not deliver a gain (source: §4.3, Prop. 2). In this deployment, SpecAgent’s value is not latency but remote usage and cost.
There is also a reason API cost does not fall as much as the token ratio. Each review resends the context as input. Strong output tokens fall to 36–50%, but with prefill input attached, cost remains at 59–81% (source: §5). This is the cost structure of a design that “replaces decode with prefill.”
4.5 Anatomy of Cost: Verification Eats Compute, Weak Eats HBM Original Fig. 3 (PDF p.10). Relative cost with Strong-only set to 1. Bars are split into Weak drafting, Strong verification, Strong repair, verification+repair, and tools/other. Strong verification and repair dominate compute but account for a small share of HBM-read.
Each bar in Fig. 3 is a ratio relative to Strong-only, and the dashed line is 1. Strong verification and repair account for 81–85% of SpecAgent FLOPs but only 39–66% of HBM-read. Conversely, Weak drafting is only 15–19% of FLOPs but uses 34–61% of HBM-read (source: Fig. 3, §5). The Weak model’s autoregressive decoding is also memory-bound. This composition explains the phenomenon that “time falls while FLOPs rise.”
Wall time has the same structure. Strong generation falls to 0.16–0.34 of Strong-only wall time, and Weak drafting adds 0.22–0.24. On VitaBench, Weak drafting adds 0.40 (source: §5). In other words, the Strong model’s long decoding is replaced by the Weak model’s short decoding plus Strong prefill.
The reason compute on VitaBench rises by as much as 1.87× is concrete. The verifier prompt and repair prompt do not share a prefix with each other, nor with the actor prompt. As a result, the Strong model prefills about 28.4k uncached tokens per task, versus 12.5k tokens for Strong-only. This prefill alone is 1.03 PFLOP, exceeding Strong-only’s total of 0.72 PFLOP, while the decode removed is only about 0.21 PFLOP (source: §5). It is a typical case of greatly increasing compute in exchange for reducing memory traffic.
The small gain on AutomationBench is also explained by the cost model. The Weak model’s drafts are rejected more often, and each rejection triggers a separate repair of about $1.5\bar d$ tokens. Thus the $c_r$ term grows, and savings shrink as the $\rho(1-p_u)$ term predicts (source: §5). VitaBench is in between. About 77% of review boundaries are rejected, but verdict and repair contribute roughly equally to the predicted ratio of 0.28 (source: §5).

Exact match demands “the same action as the Strong model,” but agent tasks have multiple valid paths. This ablation shows that the difference appears in real quality and compute.
5. Critical Comparison: Where It Wins and Where It Ties5.1 Comparison with Strong-onlySpecAgent’s strongest result is resource savings on τ². Airline ties at 86.0% quality while using 43–45% of Strong-only’s HBM-read, 41% of its wall time, and 3.1 Strong calls versus 13.8. Retail is 0.9 points behind with 53–57% of Strong-only’s HBM, 54% of its wall time, and 3.1 Strong calls versus 13.1 (source: Tab. 2). GPU·s is 2.5–5.6× lower (source: Tab. 2). This combination supports the claim that it “substantially reduces Strong decoding while nearly preserving Strong quality.”
It is difficult, however, to assert equivalent quality. Airline’s 0.0-point difference has a 95% CI of [−5.3, +5.3], and Retail’s −0.9-point difference has [−4.7, +2.9] (source: §4.2, Appx. B.1). The wide confidence intervals mean this experiment alone does not statistically establish non-inferiority. AutomationBench retains a 4.7-point gap and VitaBench a 3.5-point gap (source: Tab. 2). “Within 1 point” describes the τ² point estimates, not a guarantee across all benchmarks.
5.2 Comparison with AgentCollabOn τ², SpecAgent has higher quality and far lower resources than AgentCollab. Airline is 86.0% vs 85.3% and Retail 87.7% vs 85.7%, with 1.6–1.9× lower HBM and 2.6–3.1× lower wall time (source: §4.2, Tab. 2). AgentCollab is close to Strong quality, but its Strong calls are 18.5/16.6, far more than SpecAgent’s 3.1. That cost shows up directly in resources.
On AutomationBench, SpecAgent leads on quality at 10.5% vs 7.3% and also has lower HBM and wall time. AgentCollab uses 1.5× Strong-only’s HBM and 3.0× its wall time (source: §4.2). On VitaBench, by contrast, AgentCollab reaches 50.0%, above Strong-only’s 48.0% and 5.5 points above SpecAgent’s 44.5%. In exchange, AgentCollab uses 1.4× SpecAgent’s HBM and 1.4× its wall time (source: Tab. 2). Thus the point is not that “SpecAgent is always better” but that on VitaBench, AgentCollab is the expensive quality option and SpecAgent is the cheaper operating point.
5.3 Comparison with Speculative ActionsThe paper ports Speculative Actions to τ² and obtains 72.0% (Airline) and 48.5% (Retail). This is below Weak-only’s 80.0%/80.4%, and Strong calls are 17.4/17.1, more than Strong-only’s 13.8/13.1 (source: Tab. 2, Appx. E). The authors state, however, that these numbers come from porting the public implementation as is. The public implementation executes background tool calls in the real environment without a read-only filter and adds results to the context without checking speculated user messages against actual ones. This result should therefore be read as a property of the released implementation, not as the performance of the guarded design described in the paper (source: Appx. E). This comparison should not be overinterpreted as evidence of SpecAgent’s superiority.

6. Limitations and Risks6.1 Limitations Acknowledged by the Authors Compute does not fall. Estimated FLOPs rise by 30–38% on τ²/AutomationBench and 87% on VitaBench. The authors state that the method is suited to memory-bandwidth-bound serving (source: §1, §5). On H20, once the decode batch exceeds about 37 sequences, decode becomes compute-bound, and the FLOPs increase can turn into a time cost (source: §5). No latency gain in edge–cloud. When the local Weak model takes about as long as the hosted Strong model, the latency term in Proposition 2 does not deliver a gain. On MCP-Atlas, wall time was 105→120 seconds, 110→108 seconds, and 151→215 seconds (source: §4.3, Tab. 3). Low acceptance reduces savings. AutomationBench recovers only 44% of the quality gap, and separate repair of rejected drafts dominates cost (source: §4.2, §5). HBM numbers are estimates. Because Strong MoE expert routing is unknown, results are reported as intervals, and the Strong deployment was not validated with hardware counters. Only the Weak model received spot checks within 5–10% (source: Appx. B.4). The cost model is a first-order approximation. It assumes acceptance at each step is independent and the per-task average acceptance rate $p_u$ is constant. Real draft errors may be correlated (source: §3.3, Assumption 2). The Speculative Actions comparison is a port. It mixes in properties of the public implementation and is not a fair comparison with the guarded design (source: Appx. E). 6.2 Risks Inferred by the ReviewerThe following are the reviewer’s interpretations, not direct measurements in the paper.
Safety of false accepts. If the Strong verifier accepts an incorrect state-changing action, that error is irreversible. The paper measures success rates but does not separately report the verifier’s false accept rate and false reject rate. Whether a single review is sufficient depends on task risk (source: §3.2, §4). The assumption behind read classification. The classification that “reads do not change state” depends on benchmark documentation and observed effects. If a tool classified as a read leaves side effects such as external logs, notifications, caches, or costs, logical rollback alone is not enough. The paper also acknowledges that rejected reads may leave external traces (source: Appx. D). User-visible responses. On τ² and VitaBench, replies are not held, because they return as observations to a user turn without changing the database. However, a promise such as “I will issue your refund” is a commitment already delivered to the user. The verifier prompt instructs the model to treat this as a commit, but that is not a structural guarantee (source: Appx. D, Fig. 4). Scope of generalization. The core experiments focus on one Weak model (Qwen3.5-4B) and one main Strong model (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B). MCP-Atlas compares three Strong models, but the Weak model is fixed. Coding agents, computer use, multi-agent settings, long trajectories of more than 100 steps, and other tool ecosystems are not validated (source: §4.1, Tab. 3). Statistical evidence. The confidence intervals on τ² are wide, and paired CIs for AutomationBench/VitaBench are not reported in the main text. Point estimates alone are insufficient to claim “equivalence” or “superiority” (source: §4.2, Appx. B.1). Security and privacy. Because read tools are called speculatively with real credentials, the attack surface for access logs and data exposure grows. This risk is not quantitatively evaluated in the paper. Tool latency and queueing. The cost model ignores tool latency, and wall time is measured with 8 tasks running concurrently. Real production queueing, rate limits, and tool server latency can change the results (source: §3.3, §4.1). Truncation of review context. On VitaBench, tool results are truncated for the verifier; on MCP-Atlas, older tool results are truncated. This can create evidence the verifier misses (source: Tab. 9). 7. What’s Next?The authors’ proposed direction is clear. A stronger Weak drafter and a better-calibrated verifier translate directly into memory and latency savings without changing the protocol (source: §6). Because SpecAgent’s gain scales with acceptance, improving the Weak model’s capability and the verifier’s judgment quality is itself performance improvement.
From the reviewer’s perspective, there are four directions.
Adaptive review. Estimating per-task acceptance online and adjusting $K$ and review frequency can reduce repair cost in rejection-heavy workflows like AutomationBench. Conversely, workflows with high acceptance can allow longer chunks. Verifier calibration and safety. False accepts/rejects should be measured, and high-risk writes should combine multiple verification or tool-level transactions. Making “a single review” a structural guarantee requires managing the verifier’s error rate separately. Expanding the irreversible boundary. The current boundary is state-changing tool calls and some final messages. A design is needed that includes user-visible promises, external side effects, access logs, and personal data exposure in the boundary. Expanding deployment conditions. Validation is needed on high-batch/compute-bound serving, real HBM counters, more diverse model combinations, and coding, computer-use, and multi-agent tasks. Combining with each model’s speculative decoding or overlapping Weak/Strong asynchronously in edge–cloud are natural directions as well. 8. ConclusionSpecAgent’s core is not training a new model but changing the Strong model’s role. The Strong model becomes a reviewer of trajectories that the Weak model built on real observations, rather than the author of every step. Speculation proceeds freely while it is reversible, and verification happens only at the irreversible boundary. Acceptance is judged by semantic validity rather than exact match with the Strong model, and reviewing multiple steps in a single prefill turns Strong decoding into short verdicts and occasional repairs.
The results show that this design creates a realistic operating point. On τ² it maintains quality within 1 point of Strong-only while reducing HBM-read to 43–57% and wall time to 41–54%; on MCP-Atlas it uses only 36–50% of Strong output tokens while recovering 53–75% of the quality gap. At the same time, the 44% recovery on AutomationBench, the quality shortfall versus AgentCollab on VitaBench, the 30–87% increase in FLOPs, and the lack of latency gain in edge–cloud show that this method is a conditional optimization.
The idea that will last longest can be summarized in three sentences. Verify only at irreversible boundaries. Accept valid prefixes semantically. Amortize verification cost through prefill. The Strong model does not need to write every step, but this saving is safe only in workflows where review is cheaper than generation and where review errors are tolerable.

summary: An analysis of SpecAgent, where a weaker model drafts tool calls and a stronger model verifies them, covering its design, experimental results, and limitations.
title: Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents

content:
Paper arXiv:2610.05739 · Monash University · The University of Adelaide · Zhejiang University
One-Line Summary (TL;DR)Recurrent linear attention (Gated DeltaNet) in video world models compresses memory into a fixed-size state, which is efficient, but when the camera leaves and returns, distant scenes are progressively forgotten. HLA-WM caches chunk-level affine summaries in a training-free way and uses camera geometry (frustum overlap) to retrieve and recompose the relevant scenes, achieving PSNR +0.74 dB, rotation error −28.5%, and a 12× reduction versus Full KV in history memory over a 60-second rollout (about 6× the memory of GDN) (source: §Abstract, Fig. 1).
Key IdeaMaintaining revisit consistency requires a middle ground between a “token-level KV cache over the full history” and a “single recurrent state.” The core claim of HLA-WM is:
By exploiting the affine structure of GDN’s recurrent state transition, each time chunk is compressed into a single transition summary $(A_i, B_i)$, and at query time only the chunks overlapping the current camera geometry are selected and recomposed in temporal order, bypassing the decay introduced by irrelevant intermediate scenes.
In other words, this is a training-free technique that changes not how memory is stored but how memory is addressed and accessed (source: §1, §4.1).
Key Numbers Item Value Base model SANA-WM 1.6B (Stage-1: 4-step distilled autoregressive streaming) Context 961 frames @ 16 fps ≈ 60s, resolution 1280×704 Chunk composition 40 chunks, ≈24 camera poses per chunk Retrieval budget sink 1 + recent 1 + Top-$K$ (default $K{=}1$) Hardware Single NVIDIA H200 (140 GB) Memory (60s) HLA-WM 2.15 GiB vs Full KV 25.82 GiB vs GDN 0.359 GiB (12× reduction) Throughput loss Up to 1.6% (Stage-1 FPS 22.403 → 22.053) Background: the Problem They SolvedA world model predicts the dynamics of an environment so that an agent can simulate future observations and the consequences of its actions. Recent video world models implement this via autoregressive generation conditioned on camera trajectories or actions (source: §1). To go beyond short-term temporal continuity and achieve long-horizon simulation, past scenes outside the recent context must remain recoverable later. When the camera returns, the model must restore the earlier scene structure rather than produce a semantically similar but spatially inconsistent view (source: §1).
Here two extremes diverge:
Softmax attention + Full KV cache: Direct access to the entire history, but the storage cost keeps growing in proportion to the rollout length (source: §1, Fig. 4). Recurrent linear attention: Compresses the history into a fixed-size state, so memory is cheap, but distant information is vulnerable to decay and interference from subsequent updates (source: §2). The authors quantitatively capture the long-range forgetting problem in Gated DeltaNet (GDN). GDN’s chunk-level recurrent transition is:
$$S_i = S_{i-1}A_i + B_i,$$where $A_i$ is the state transition applied to past memory and $B_i$ is the information newly written by the current chunk. Unrolling this across several chunks gives (source: §3, Eq. 1–2)
$$S_j = \cdots + B_i\,A_{i+1}A_{i+2}\cdots A_j + \cdots + B_j,$$that is, the information $B_i$ written by an early chunk $i$ must pass through every subsequent transition matrix in turn before it can influence a distant $j$. The authors measure this decay with an average norm:
$$W_{i\to j} = \mathrm{AvgNorm}(A_{i+1}A_{i+2}\cdots A_j).$$The result is dramatic. In a representative trajectory, the camera leaves the Chunk 3 region, makes a large loop, and returns to a nearby viewpoint at Chunk 35; the retained influence of Chunk 3, $W_{3\to 35}$, drops to 0.0416 (source: Fig. 2). Chunk 3 and Chunk 35 see a region with large overlap, but the irrelevant intermediate viewpoints in between successively multiply the transitions and repeatedly distort the original memory.
Key insight: GDN memory is updated according to “the passage of time,” but in a world model the relevance of information is determined not by time but by spatial/geometric proximity. This mismatch is the root cause of forgetting (source: §3).
New Approach: HLA-WMHLA-WM replaces the single accumulated GDN memory with a collection of independently addressable per-chunk memories (source: §4.1). It consists of three stages.
Per-chunk GDN memory — Cache each time chunk as a single affine transition summary $(A_i, B_i)$. Geometry-based retrieval — Compute a frustum overlap score from the camera pose, intrinsics, and scene median depth to select relevant chunks. Selective state recomposition — Compose the selected summaries in temporal order to produce a query-specific recurrent state. How It Works: A Concrete Walkthrough1) GDN’s affine structure. The token-level GDN update is (source: §4.2, Eq. 4):
$$S_t = \gamma_t S_{t-1} + \beta_t (v_t - S_{t-1}k_t)\, k_t^{\top},$$where $k_t, v_t$ are the key and value projected from the current token, $\gamma_t$ is the memory decay, and $\beta_t$ is the delta update strength. Rearranging this gives the affine form $S_t = S_{t-1}A_t + B_t$, with
$$A_t = \gamma_t I - \beta_t k_t k_t^{\top},\qquad B_t = \beta_t v_t k_t^{\top}.$$Unrolling the $L$ tokens within a chunk $i$, the entire chunk can be represented by a single affine transition $(A_i, B_i)$. These summaries satisfy the associative law (source: Eq. 9):
$$(A_i, B_i) \star (A_j, B_j) = (A_i A_j,\; B_i A_j + B_j).$$This is the crux. Thanks to the associative law, any subset of history chunks can be recomposed efficiently without re-running the original visual tokens (source: §4.2).
2) Geometry retrieval. The overlap between each query chunk $q$ and history chunk $i$ is estimated from camera geometry alone, not from RGB or learned features. At a sampled pixel location $(u,v)$, the camera-space ray is formed as
$$r(u,v) = \Big[\tfrac{u-c_x}{f_x},\ \tfrac{v-c_y}{f_y},\ 1\Big]^{\top}$$and 3D points are scattered at three proxy depths around the scene median depth, $D = \{0.5d_{\text{med}}, d_{\text{med}}, 1.5d_{\text{med}}\}$, then projected into the camera view of the relative chunk to obtain the visible ratio $V$. The symmetric frustum overlap score is (source: §4.3, Eq. 12)
$$R(i,q) = \tfrac{1}{2}\big[V(i \to q) + V(q \to i)\big].$$3) Selection and recomposition. The first chunk is always retained as a sink, the recent chunks preserve local continuity, and the top $K$ of the remaining history by $R(i,q)$ are selected (source: Eq. 13)
$$I_q = I_{\text{sink}} \cup I_{\text{recent}} \cup \underset{i \in H_q}{\mathrm{TopK}}\; R(i,q),$$and the selected chunks are sorted in temporal order and composed to produce the query-specific history state (source: Eq. 17):
$$S_q^{\text{hist}} = S_0\, A_{\pi_q} + B_{\pi_q}.$$Concrete example. Return to the loop trajectory of Fig. 2. The camera goes Chunk 3 (first visit) → Chunk 4–34 (irrelevant distant departure) → Chunk 35 (revisit). When building $S_{35}$, the existing GDN passes the information written by Chunk 3 through the roughly 32 transitions of Chunk 4–34 in turn, eroding it down to $W_{3\to 35} = 0.0416$. HLA-WM, by contrast, detects when generating Chunk 35 that the frustum overlap with Chunk 3, $R(3, 35)$, is high, and selects Chunk 3’s summary $(A_3, B_3)$ along with the sink and recent context, composing them while skipping the transitions of Chunk 4–34. This vastly reduces the number of irrelevant transitions a distant but relevant memory is exposed to before reuse (source: §4.4).
Performance Validation: Main ResultsExperiments were run on SANA-WM-Bench (80 trajectories each for simple/hard, 4 scene categories) and MBench-A (547 samples, 4 subsets), with the official 1.6B SANA-WM as the base model. HLA-WM modifies only the Stage-1 memory mechanism and does no fine-tuning (source: §5.1).
SANA-WM-Bench. In Stage-1 (the stage that directly modifies recurrent memory), HLA-WM improves both revisit consistency and camera control metrics across both splits (source: §5.2, Tab. 1):
| Pipeline | Metric | SANA-WM | HLA-WM | Δ | |—|—:|—:|—:| | Hard · Stage-1 | PSNR ↑ | 9.37 dB | 10.11 dB | +0.74 dB | | Hard · Stage-1 | SSIM ↑ | 0.1774 | 0.1997 | +0.0223 | | Hard · Stage-1 | LPIPS ↓ | 0.6044 | 0.5848 | −0.0196 | | Hard · Stage-1 | RotErr ↓ | 20.38° | 15.09° | −26.0% | | Simple · Stage-1 | PSNR ↑ | 9.18 dB | 9.91 dB | +0.73 dB | | Simple · Stage-1 | RotErr ↓ | 19.70° | 13.59° | −31.0% |
That is, the abstract’s headline numbers “PSNR +0.74 dB, rotation error −28.5%” combine the Stage-1 results for Hard (+0.74 dB, −26.0%) and Simple (−31.0%) (source: §Abstract, §5.2). Interestingly, the camera control metrics also improve. Preserved scene geometry reduces structural drift, providing a more stable spatial reference for camera-conditioned generation (source: §5.2).
Retained after downstream refinement. In bidirectional refinement all six metrics improve (PSNR +0.52/+0.46 dB, RotErr −22.0%/−20.1%), and revisit consistency improves consistently under causal AR refinement as well. However, in the refinement stage there is a trade-off in which some metrics worsen slightly depending on the mode (TransErr and CamMC for Simple) (source: §5.2, Tab. 1).
Generalization: MBench-A. Across all 547 samples, PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS improve consistently in all three inference modes. In Stage-1 the largest gains appear: PSNR +0.84 dB, SSIM +0.0303, LPIPS −0.0428 (source: §5.2, Tab. 2). The gains are not concentrated in a specific subset; all three metrics improve simultaneously across all 12 mode–subset combinations (source: Appx. A.8.2).
Efficiency. HLA-WM offers a practical compromise between Full KV attention and recurrent linear attention. Because the history is cached in chunks rather than tokens, memory scales with the number of chunks rather than the number of tokens. On a 60-second context it uses only 2.15 GiB (a 12× reduction over Full KV) while incurring a throughput loss of at most 1.6% (source: §5.2, Fig. 4).
Key ablations. The authors answer two questions (source: Appx. A.3–A.5).
Which components matter? Removing the sink, disabling transition selection (“w/o Select A”), disabling write selection (“w/o Select B”), and removing turn-aware recent context all degrade revisit consistency and camera control. In particular, leaving in irrelevant intermediate transitions drops PSNR and SSIM substantially, supporting the claim that “irrelevant transitions are the cause of forgetting” (source: Appx. A.3, Tab. 3). Which matters more, GDN recomposition or KV alignment? GDN-only yields a far larger gain than KV-only, and combining the two gives the best performance. In the Hard trajectories of bidirectional refinement, GDN-only raises SSIM but worsens RotErr from 13.17° to 33.04°, showing a “memory-path mismatch”; applying the same selection to the KV cache stabilizes it again (source: Appx. A.4, Tab. 4). Retrieval budget and selection strategy. Surprisingly, $K{=}1$ (the single most relevant history chunk) is best on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Retrieving more gives no consistent improvement (source: Appx. A.5, Tab. 6). Also, geometry-based selection gives better revisit consistency than heuristics such as Random, Recent, and Uniform, showing that beyond “broad temporal coverage,” explicitly choosing view-relevant history provides additional benefit (source: Appx. A.6, Tab. 7).
Effect of revisit interval. The gain grows with the revisit interval (PSNR improvement rises from +0.375 dB at short intervals <10s to +0.992 dB at long intervals ≥40s). This result aligns exactly with the method’s intent: the benefit of selective long-term memory is most pronounced for the “heavily forgotten” long-range revisits (source: Appx. A.7, Fig. 6).
Our Perspective: Strengths, Limitations, and Why This Work MattersStrengths. The most striking aspect is the practicality of being training-free. It leaves the pretrained 1.6B model untouched and only changes how memory is accessed at inference time to raise long-range consistency. Exploiting GDN’s affine structure analytically to scale memory as $O(\text{chunks})$ rather than $O(\text{tokens})$ while simultaneously achieving a 12× reduction and a throughput loss of around 1.6% is a strong demonstration of the viability of the idea of “selectively addressable recurrent memory” (source: §4.4, Fig. 4). The GDN-only vs KV-only ablation, which isolates that “recurrent state recomposition is the main driver,” is also analytically clean (source: Appx. A.4).
Limitations. As the authors explicitly acknowledge, the training-free property itself constrains the ceiling. Retrieval relies only on camera geometry and FOV overlap and does not model occlusion, visibility, or semantic relevance (source: §6). We would point to three additional limitations. First, retrieval assumes a prescribed camera trajectory, whereas in open-loop generation by a real agent the pose must be estimated separately, and that error propagates into retrieval quality. Second, the “fixed 24-frame chunk” and “sink 1 + recent 1 + Top-1” design are values tuned on the specific SANA-WM-Bench and MBench-A pipelines, so robustness to different chunking and fps remains open. Third, the result that $K{=}1$ is optimal also means, conversely, that “richer retrieval does not help,” suggesting a representational limit in the retrieval signal itself (source: Appx. A.5).
Why this work matters. This paper connects the LLM KV-cache compression and long-context literature with the video world model literature. On the spectrum between a “full history cache” and a “single compressed state,” it offers a third point — selective recomposition using geometric information as an addressing signal — and shows that it works without training. As video world models grow longer, “how to address memory” will become the bottleneck, and this paper provides one concrete, measurable answer to that question.
What’s Next?: The Road AheadThe authors propose integrating selective state retrieval into training and richer or learned retrieval signals that include occlusion, visibility, and semantic relevance as future directions (source: §6). Beyond these, the directions we would look forward to are as follows.
Combining with a learned router. For now, camera geometry is a “free” addressing signal, but it has limits for semantic revisits (the reappearance of the same object rather than the same place). A hybrid in which geometric signals serve as a prior and a lightweight router corrects them is natural. Occlusion-aware retrieval. Frustum overlap cannot see “behind walls.” Adding depth-buffer or occupancy signals could reduce occlusion errors in indoor scenes. Automating chunking and the retrieval budget. Instead of a fixed 24 frames and Top-1, dynamically adjusting the chunk size and $K$ based on scene change rate or motion magnitude could achieve a better efficiency–quality trade-off. Deeper optimization of the recomposition kernel. The forward scan the authors implemented on top of a Triton kernel is a starting point. Batching and memory-layout optimizations could reduce that 1.6% throughput loss further (source: §4.4, Appx. A.2). In summary, HLA-WM starts from a clear diagnosis of “the forgetting of recurrent linear attention,” offers an elegant and practical solution — geometry-based selective recomposition — and robustly validates its effectiveness on two benchmarks. By driving this much long-range consistency improvement without any training, this work will be an important stepping stone toward efficient long-horizon world models.

title: HLA-WM: Hybrid Linear Attention for Long-Horizon Video World Models

content:
Paper TL;DR — Parallel diffusion drafters like DFlash produce a whole block of tokens at once, but within the block they predict each token without knowing the identity of the preceding tokens. DCOCO is a lightweight corrector that re-selects contextually appropriate tokens by scoring the adjacent transitions among already-drafted candidates in a single batched operation, with no extra drafter forward pass. Across 4 backbones and 10 benchmarks it is up to 6.6× faster than vanilla and up to 18% faster than the strongest speculative baseline, and it retains a 6–23% margin even at concurrency of 4–32 streams.
Core IdeaSpeculative decoding accelerates LLM inference with the idea that “a lightweight drafter proposes tokens and a heavy target model verifies them in one pass.” The problem is the tension between drafting speed and acceptance rate.
The authors focus on exactly one thing. The currently popular parallel drafters (which predict an entire block at once in a diffusion-based manner, as DFlash does) are fast, but within a block they do not see the actual selection made in the preceding slot. As a result, tokens that look plausible individually combine to simultaneously assign high probability to “New York” and “San Diego,” producing an unnatural continuation like “New Diego” (§2). This lowers the acceptance rate and ultimately erodes the speed gain.
Existing methods such as DSpark and Domino try to solve this problem with a sequential module, but that sequential module sits on the critical path of every decoding cycle. DCOCO (DFlash Contextual Corrector) answers “yes” to the question of whether intra-block dependencies can be restored without reintroducing a sequential module (§1).
The key lies in two observations.
The drafter already has the answer. For Qwen3-8B, in 59% of slots where top-1 is wrong, the verifier’s actual token is present among the top-16 candidates (§2). Correction can therefore be reduced not to “generating new tokens” but to re-selection among candidates that already exist. Verification stops at the front. Speculative verification accepts only a contiguous prefix and halts at the first rejection. Improving later slots therefore matters only if all earlier slots are accepted, so correction must concentrate on the quality of the early prefix (§2). Combining these two turns the corrector into the following task: “keep the top $K$ candidates per slot, score all $K^2$ transitions between adjacent slots in parallel, then greedily choose from the front.” The decisive difference from DSpark and Domino is that neural scoring is parallel and only the selection is sequential (a simple walk over the grid).
Background: the Problem They SolvedStructure of Speculative DecodingThe verifier scores the proposed block $\hat y_{1:B}$ in a single forward pass, decides slots from left to right, commits the longest accepted prefix, and then adds one token of its own. Under greedy decoding, slot $j$ is accepted if it matches the verifier’s greedy choice; under stochastic decoding it is accepted by the standard speculative sampling rule $\min\{1, q_j(\hat y_j)/p_j(\hat y_j)\}$ (§3.1).
Writing the acceptance of slot $j$ as $a_j\in\{0,1\}$, the acceptance length is
$$ A(\hat y) = \max\{ m : a_1 = a_2 = \dots = a_m = 1 \}, $$and each round commits $A(\hat y)+1$ tokens. Throughput is ultimately determined by the expected acceptance length and the wall-clock time per round. And this single structural fact — “verification stops at the first rejection” — governs every design choice in DCOCO, because if slot 1 is rejected, the corrected token in slot 5 is never even examined (§3.1).
Candidate Coverage: the Missed HeadroomThe authors recorded DFlash’s candidates during $T{=}0$ speculative decoding and compared them against the actual continuation to measure top-$k$ coverage — “the fraction of draft slots whose top-$k$ candidates contain the token the verifier ultimately commits” (§2).
The results are regular. On Qwen3-8B, at the first slot top-16 is about 95.1% and top-1 (the drafter’s own choice) is 81.4%, a small gap, but at the last slot top-16 is still 60.8% while top-1 falls to 15.4% (Fig. 1, Tab. 7). Averaged over the whole block, top-1 is 40.0% vs top-16 75.5%. That is, at deep slots nearly one in two slots has the correct answer in its candidate pool, yet the drafter increasingly fails to pick it. This “missed correct answer” is exactly the headroom the corrector re-selects from.
The New Approach: DCOCODCOCO operates in two stages. (1) Given the realized tokens, it re-assigns a stronger contextual score to the drafter’s per-slot candidates, and (2) it re-selects the block according to those scores (§3).
1) A Learned Corrector over the Block GridAt each slot $i\in\{1,\dots,B\}$, DFlash leaves a hidden state $h_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and the top $K$ candidates. Here $c_{ik}$ is the token id of the $k$-th candidate at slot $i$, and $\ell_i(k)$ is its draft logit. These candidates form a dense first-order grid of $B\times K$ nodes, with every candidate at slot $p$ connected to every candidate at slot $p+1$.
Each transition is assigned a score:
$$ S_p(a,b) = \underbrace{\ell_{p+1}(b)}_{\text{draft unary logit}} + \underbrace{\Delta_\theta(s_p,\, z_{pa},\, z_{p+1,b},\, \ell_p(a),\, \ell_{p+1}(b))}_{\text{learned correction}}, $$where $\Delta_\theta$ is a shared 2-layer MLP, $z_{ik}$ is a candidate representation, and $s_p$ is a candidate-independent pair state (§3.2). The corrector reads only the hidden states, candidate ids, and logits left by a single DFlash pass.
Candidate representation $z_{ik}$: it fuses $b_{ik}$, obtained by projecting and normalizing the embedding of $c_{ik}$ from the frozen token embedding table $E$, with $g_i$, obtained by projecting and normalizing the slot hidden state $h_i$, via concatenation. Because the token embedding and hidden state differ in scale by more than two orders of magnitude, it uses a non-affine layer normalization. Pair state $s_p$: it concatenates the hidden states of adjacent slots, $s_p = W_{\text{pair}}[h_p; h_{p+1}]$. Since $s_p$ depends only on slots, it is computed once and reused across all $K^2$ transitions between them. There are two key design tricks. First, the MLP’s output layer is initialized to zero, so initially $\Delta_\theta\equiv 0$ and every transition score reduces to the successor’s draft logit $S_p(a,b)=\ell_{p+1}(b)$, thereby reproducing the drafter’s original proposal exactly at initialization (§3.2). Second, all projection and MLP parameters are shared across slots and transitions, and the $(B-1)K^2$ transition scores are computed in a single batched operation before path selection.
2) Prefix-first Greedy SelectionOn the scored grid, simply maximizing the total path score lets high scores at later slots compensate for low scores at earlier ones — but later tokens contribute only if the earlier prefix survives. Because of this asymmetry, DCOCO uses a prefix-first greedy rule:
$$ k_1 = \arg\max_k \ell_1(k), \qquad k_{p+1} = \arg\max_b S_p(k_p, b) \quad (p=1,\dots,B-1). $$The first slot keeps the drafter’s top candidate, and each subsequent slot picks its successor only from scores conditioned on the selected predecessor. The absence of lookahead into future transitions is actually an advantage: this walk costs only $O(BK)$ (added on top of the $O(BK^2)$ scoring), and if $\Delta_\theta\equiv 0$ it agrees exactly with the drafter’s argmax (§3.3).
3) Training: Supervise Only on Verifier-Correct PrefixesThe drafter and corrector are optimized jointly. The label $(a^\star_p, b^\star_p)$ for transition $p$ is the pair of verifier argmax tokens at the two slots under a teacher-forced context, and it is activated with mask $m_p=1$ only when it lies within each slot’s top-$K$. The correction loss multiplies a cross-entropy, normalized over the $K^2$ transitions by a joint softmax, by an exponential decay weight:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{corr}} \propto -\sum_{p=1}^{B-1} e^{-(p-1)/\rho}\, m_p \log \frac{\exp S_p(a^\star_p, b^\star_p)}{\sum_{a,b=1}^{K}\exp S_p(a,b)}, \qquad \rho = 4. $$This softmax exists only during training; at inference time $S_p$ is used without normalization. The exponential weight is a fixed proxy reflecting the prefix-survival structure — “a later transition contributes only if the earlier slot is accepted” (§3.2, App. A). The supervision simply drops rather than suppresses transitions the drafter finds unreachable, since the verifier-correct prefix is the only state in which the corrector’s output is actually consumed (App. A).
4) Deterministic Proposals Even Under Stochastic DecodingThis is an interesting theoretical result. DCOCO selects tokens deterministically even under stochastic decoding, so each slot’s proposal distribution becomes a point mass $p_j(v)=\mathbf{1}[v=\hat y_j]$. The acceptance probability of standard speculative sampling then simplifies to $\min\{1, q_j/p_j\}=q_j(\hat y_j)$, and on rejection the residual distribution becomes $r_j(v)=q_j(v)\mathbf{1}[v\neq\hat y_j]/(1-q_j(\hat y_j))$. Repeating this at every slot preserves the verifier distribution exactly — that is, stochastic target decoding does not require stochastic draft selection (App. D). No softmax normalization on transition scores and no candidate-distribution sampling are needed.
How It Works: Walking Through a Concrete ExampleLet us reproduce the “New Diego” problem in miniature. Say the block size is $B=4$ and the number of candidates per slot is $K=3$. Suppose a single DFlash pass left the following (the same example tokens and scores as Fig. 2 in the paper).
Slot 1: These(4.2), The(3.6), A(2.8) Slot 2: key(0.4), keys(2.7), locks(1.1) Slot 3: is(0.2), are(3.1), was(0.8) Slot 4: missing(2.8), here(1.6), broken(0.5) If the drafter simply picks each slot’s top-1, the result is “These key is missing” — every word is plausible, yet the grammar is off. The identity of the problem is that the adjacent context — that “These” should be followed by “keys” and “keys” by “are” — is not reflected in the drafter at all.
DCOCO lays this block out into a $4\times 3$ grid. It builds each slot’s candidate representation $z_{ik}$ (embedding + slot hidden state) and pair state $s_p$, and scores all $3\times 3=9$ transitions between adjacent slots with the shared MLP $\Delta_\theta$. For instance, the 9 transitions of (Slot1→Slot2) are all computed in parallel as:
$$ S_1(\text{These}, b) = \ell_2(b) + \Delta_\theta(s_1, z_{1,\text{These}}, z_{2,b}, \dots) $$Since during training $\Delta_\theta$ was trained to assign high scores to adjacent pairs that the verifier actually selects, such as “These + keys” and “keys + are,” it adds a correction to the draft logit $\ell_2(\text{key})=0.4$ so that $S_1(\text{These}, \text{keys})$ overtakes $S_1(\text{These}, \text{key})$.
Then comes the prefix-first walk. Slot 1 is fixed to top-1 These (→ These). Slot 2 picks keys, which maximizes $S_1(\text{These}, \cdot)$ (→ These keys). Slot 3 now picks are, which maximizes $S_2(\text{keys}, \cdot)$ conditioned on the selected keys (→ These keys are). Finally, Slot 4 picks missing via $S_3(\text{are}, \cdot)$. The final proposal is “These keys are missing” — an ungrammatical string produced by the drafter’s top-1 combination has been turned into a grammatically correct sentence with no extra drafter forward pass.
The important point here is that only the selection is sequential, while the 9 scorings are all bundled into a single batched operation. To fix this example, DSpark and Domino must run a recurrent module that sweeps slot by slot, whereas DCOCO finishes with one parallel scoring plus an $O(BK)$ walk.
Performance Validation: Main ResultsSetupThe verifiers are four backbones — Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, Llama-3.1-8B — and the benchmarks are 10 covering math (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME-25), code (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench), and general (MT-Bench, Arena-Hard-v2, Alpaca, SpeedBench). All drafters were trained with block size 16 on about 800K prompts (stem/math/code from Nemotron Post-Training v2 + CodeAlpaca-20k). Serving uses vLLM 0.27.0 on a single NVIDIA B200, BF16, TP=1 (App. C). The primary metric is end-to-end tokens per second (TPS), and the secondary metric is the average acceptance length $\tau$, which separates “quality improvement” from “serving overhead” (§4).
Why Accepted Length and Actual Throughput Must Be Read TogetherThe most honest choice in this paper is making TPS the primary metric. The corrector can increase acceptance length while eroding wall-clock time with its own scoring cost, and that trade-off shows up only in TPS (§4). The paper therefore reports $\tau$ (mechanism) and TPS (outcome) side by side.
On Qwen3-8B (thinking off), DCOCO achieves an average acceptance length $\tau$ of 4.985, which is +8.1% over Domino (4.613), +17.2% over DSpark (4.254), and +27.4% over uncorrected DFlash (3.913). And this $\tau$ improvement translates directly into a TPS improvement (Fig. 3, Tab. 2).
Overall Results: First Place in All 12 CellsIn all 12 combinations of four backbones × (thinking on/off) × ($T{=}0$/$T{=}1$), DCOCO recorded the best average speedup (§4.1, Tab. 2). In each cell it leads the strongest baseline by 8–19%. For Qwen3-8B, math and code benchmarks go up to 3.7–6.1× over vanilla, while open-ended chat is 1.8–1.9× (greedy decoding). The up to 6.6× in the abstract comes from Qwen3-4B on AIME-25.
Averaging over the 10 suites for Qwen3-8B (thinking off, $T{=}0$):
System Avg TPS vs vanilla No-spec(vanilla) 265.6 1.0× DFlash(uncorrected) 783.1 2.95× DSpark 765.6 2.88× Domino 839.3 3.16× DCOCO 959.7 3.62× That is, it is 14.3% faster than the strongest competing corrector Domino and 22.6% faster than uncorrected DFlash (Tab. 1).
The Decisive Difference Revealed Under ConcurrencyLLM serving batches concurrent requests to raise GPU utilization. As concurrency grows, the verifier’s cycle time is amortized across streams, so the share of overhead the corrector adds per cycle keeps growing. This is exactly the graveyard of sequential correctors.
On Qwen3-8B (thinking off), DCOCO records the highest throughput across the entire range of concurrency from 4 to 32 streams, with a margin over the strongest baseline of +16.6%→+23.0% at $T{=}0$ and +16.1%→+12.4% at $T{=}1$ (Tab. 8). By contrast, Domino and DSpark keep an almost unchanged acceptance length, yet accumulate sequential-correction overhead and eventually become slower than uncorrected DFlash.
Fig. 3 makes this phenomenon clear. The vertical axis is the ratio relative to DFlash, the solid line is the acceptance length $\tau$, the dashed line is throughput, and the shaded region is the gap between them (= the corrector’s per-cycle overhead). Domino’s $\tau$ curve stays above parity (1.0), but its throughput curve slides below — overhead has swallowed the acceptance gain. In contrast, DCOCO’s two curves move nearly together with a thin shaded region and remain above parity. This phenomenon reproduces across all four backbones (App. B).
Path Selection and AblationComparing path selection rules (§4.3) on the same learned score grid, Global-Sum (maximizing the total sum) yields lower $\tau$ and TPS than greedy on all 9 suites. Geometric discount ($\lambda=0.75$) is comparable to greedy in acceptance length (average 5.258 vs 5.254), but greedy achieves +2.8% on average higher throughput. In the end, greedy wins with its $O(BK)$ walk and no discount hyperparameter (Tab. 3).
Ablation (App. A) validates the corrector’s two input paths.
Removing the pair state: acceptance length $-$7.3%/$-$5.6% ($T{=}0$/$T{=}1$), throughput $-$6.3%/$-$4.6%. Removing the candidate representation: acceptance length $-$4.8%/$-$3.7%, throughput $-$4.6%/$-$3.3%. Freezing the backbone (fixing the drafter for 6 epochs and training only the corrector): throughput $-$15.9%/$-$12.9%. That is, both input paths are essential, and their contribution is largest on math and code. Co-adaptation is also key: even with a frozen backbone the corrector is a pure drop-in that yields +4.4% TPS over DFlash, but it is 15.9% below joint training. Conversely, extending the baselines to 12 epochs improves them by no more than 2%, confirming that DCOCO’s gain comes from the corrector itself, not from “training budget” (Tab. 4).
Our Take: Strengths, Limitations, and Why This Research MattersStrengths A clean answer to “restoring dependencies without sequencing.” Whereas DSpark and Domino take the compromise of “parallel draft + sequential correction,” DCOCO revives dependencies without sacrificing parallelism. The separation of fully parallel neural scoring with only an $O(BK)$ selection walk is this paper’s most elegant contribution (§1, §3). Redefining the problem as “re-selection.” It is decisive that correction is reduced not to “generating new tokens” but to “re-selecting among the existing top-$K$ candidates.” The measurement of top-16 coverage 75.5% vs top-1 40.0% (Fig. 1) shows that this redefinition is not vacuous but grounded in real headroom. Honesty about metrics. The design of using TPS as the primary metric and $\tau$ as the mechanism metric probes exactly the trap of correctors that “raise acceptance length but lose in wall-clock time.” The fact that the concurrency experiment demonstrates this trade-off makes the paper’s conclusion a system-level claim, not a single benchmark number. Low cost. On Qwen3-8B the corrector is only about 2.23M parameters (drafter $d=4096$, 5 layers), and its per-cycle cost is merely 3–4% over uncorrected (App. A, §4.1). The concluding sentence “a correction made cheap enough is pure profit” is backed by the numbers. Limitations Single GPU, single framework. All experiments were performed on a single NVIDIA B200 + vLLM 0.27.0 + TP=1 (§4, App. C). Behavior under multi-GPU tensor parallelism or other runtimes (e.g., TRT-LLM) is unverified. Single-seed training. Each method was trained once with seed 42, and variance across training seeds was not measured (App. A). The standard deviation for $T{=}1$ is only over “3 generation seeds,” not variability across independent training runs. Room to argue over baseline fairness. Comparisons use “each method’s native configuration,” and DCOCO uses 6+6 epochs (drafter 6 + joint 6) whereas the baselines use 6 epochs. The authors defend fairness by showing that extended training gives the baselines less than 2% gain (Tab. 4), but this can still be a point of contention for readers demanding “exactly the same block size and the same budget.” Drafter dependence. DCOCO is built on top of a specific parallel drafter, DFlash. Transfer to other parallel/diffusion drafters is natural but not empirically demonstrated, and sensitivity sweeps for hyperparameters such as block size, $K$, and $\rho$ are limited. Limits on open-ended chat. Math and code speed up to 3.7–6.1×, but open-ended chat like MT-Bench and Alpaca stays at 1.8–1.9× (§4.1). This is a limitation of the drafter’s base acceptance rate itself, a structure DCOCO amplifies rather than overcomes. Why It MattersThe real contribution of this research is not a specific number but a perspective that flips the problem. It replaces the implicit premise that “reversing the weakness of parallel drafting (intra-block independence) requires sequencing” with “the correct answer is already in the candidate pool, and scoring adjacent transitions in parallel restores it without sequencing.” And by showing that this replacement shines even under concurrent load — indeed all the more so — it draws the practical conclusion that “making correction cheap is the pure profit of speculative decoding.” At a time when speculative decoding is becoming standard in real serving stacks, this approach, which fills the last weakness of parallel drafting, is worth attention.
What’s Next?: The Road AheadThe authors do not explicitly lay out a grand future roadmap, but next steps follow naturally from the paper’s limitations and structure.
Generalization to other drafters and backends. The most direct task is to verify whether DCOCO’s “parallel scoring + prefix-first walk” still holds an advantage on parallel drafters other than DFlash (e.g., other diffusion/CTC-based ones) and under multi-GPU and other runtimes. Systematic sweeps of $K$, block size, and $\rho$. The number of top-$K$ candidates and the exponential decay $\rho$ are the knobs that directly control the trade-off between “candidate headroom” and “scoring cost.” Quantifying their cost-acceptance curves would yield tuning guidance for deployment. Adaptive candidate counts. It is promising to exploit the fact that coverage drops sharply with slot depth (Fig. 1) in reverse, reducing scoring cost by using a small $K$ for shallow slots and a large $K$ for deep slots. Acceptance-rate-based training weights. The current exponential weight with $\rho=4$ is a “fixed proxy” for prefix survival. Estimating actual acceptance probabilities and making the per-position training weights data-adaptive is the logical follow-up (explicitly mentioned in §3.2). Designs targeting batch serving. Since the concurrency experiment already shows that correction overhead is the deciding variable, system optimizations that fuse scoring more finely at the CUDA-kernel level or exploit shared computation within a mini-batch will be the source of the next gain. In short, DCOCO has offered a new baseline for speculative decoding: “the cheapest way to recover the lost context of parallel drafting.” What comes next will be extending this idea to more diverse hardware, drafters, and load conditions to draw the boundary of the proposition that “correction is always pure profit.”
