Paper Phase Sensitivity: The ‘Periodic Weakness’ Created by Chunked KV-Cache Compression TL;DR — In models that use chunked KV-cache compression (such as the DeepSeek-V4 family), the same information can vary in retrieval performance by up to 40pp periodically depending on its ‘phase’ relative to the compression window boundary. Average benchmark scores completely hide this weakness.
Core IdeaThe bottleneck of long-context reasoning is the KV cache. Memory and attention costs grow in proportion to context length (source: §1). To address this, models like DeepSeek-V4 use chunked KV-cache compression. Consecutive tokens are grouped into fixed-size windows, each window is summarized into a smaller number of cache entries, and long-range retrieval is performed using those summaries (source: §1).
The insight of this paper starts here. Compression forces a periodic structure in which a new window begins every $S$ tokens onto the context. $S$ is the compression stride. Each token then acquires a new coordinate besides absolute position: its phase (source: §1):
$$\text{phase} = t \bmod S$$Merely shifting the input by a few tokens leaves the content and relative positions unchanged, yet which tokens get grouped into the same window changes. That is, the same information is compressed differently depending on phase, and can therefore be preserved with different fidelity.
The authors define it this way. For stride $S$, the phase of the key-value pair starting at position $t$ is $t \bmod S$. When some retrieval metric (accuracy, probability of the correct answer, etc.) varies systematically with the phase of the information, retrieval is said to exhibit phase sensitivity (source: §2).
The core claim is summarized in this one sentence. “In models that use chunked KV-cache compression, there exists a periodic retrieval failure (periodic weakness) invisible in average scores, and its period matches the compression stride.”
Background: The Problem They SolvedThe cost of the KV cache grows in proportion to context length. Roughly, for a model with $L$ layers, $H$ heads, and head dimension $d_\text{head}$, at sequence length $\text{seq}$ and batch size $\text{batch}$, the cache size grows as follows:
$$ \text{KV-Cache(GB)} \approx \frac{2 \cdot L \cdot H \cdot d_\text{head} \cdot \text{seq} \cdot \text{batch} \cdot \text{bytes/elt}}{10^9} $$The family of learned compression memory approaches emerged to reduce this cost. Compressive Transformer, LoMA, Activation Beacon, CAT, along with sparse attention (NSA, MOBA, DeepSeek-V4’s CSA) and cache eviction (H2O, SnapKV), all share the same goal (source: §6).
Yet existing evaluation methods have a blind spot. “Lost in the Middle” showed that depth in the context determines retrieval quality, and RULER showed that easy needle tests overestimate the practically usable context length (source: §6). What this paper focuses on is an entirely different dimension. Not the context depth or query position of information, but its phase relative to compression window boundaries — a microscopic coordinate that repeats every stride.
What the authors found is surprising. The retrieval performance of the same information fluctuates periodically with this phase. And this is completely masked by average metrics.
New Approach: Phase Sensitivity + Phase SpecializationThis paper does not propose a new model or a new architecture. Instead, it is an analysis paper that defines a new failure mode and identifies its origin mechanistically and theoretically. The contributions fall broadly into three categories (source: §1, §3, §4, §5).
Identification of a new failure mode (empirical discovery). It is the first to report ‘phase sensitivity,’ in which retrieval accuracy varies periodically with phase in chunked KV compression models. It reproduces in DeepSeek-V4, V4.1, and in all compression models the authors pretrained themselves.
Mechanism identification (causal intervention). Through causal interventions such as KV head knockout and gate cycling, it demonstrates phase specialization, in which different heads contribute asymmetrically to retrieval at different phases.
Theoretical explanation (optimization dynamics). On an idealized bigram retrieval task, it shows that concentration of the compression gate is the optimum, and proves as a theorem that gradient flow freezes that concentration statically.
What sets this apart from prior work is that it abandons the lens of ‘average accuracy.’ It digs into the fact that, even when benchmark scores are the same, a periodically repeating positional failure hides within.
How It Works: A Concrete ExampleHow Chunk Compression Is DoneThe compression kernel used in the controlled experiments makes the behavior clear (source: §3). Let the hidden state at offset $i$ ($0 \le i < W$) in window $j$ of window size $W$ be $h_{j,i} \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Each offset determines “what to contribute” via a payload map $C_i$, and “how strongly to enter” via compression gates $Z_i$, $b_i$. In the key branch, the gate logit is:
$$ s_{j,i}^{K} = Z_{i}^{K} h_{j,i} + b_{i}^{K} $$A softmax is taken over the whole window to produce gate scores, which are multiplied against the payload and summed:
$$ \alpha_{j,i}^{K} = \frac{\exp(s_{j,i}^{K})}{\sum_{u=0}^{W-1} \exp(s_{j,u}^{K})}, \qquad \widehat{K}_j = \sum_{i=0}^{W-1} \alpha_{j,i}^{K} \odot \left( C_i^K h_{j,i} \right) $$The key point is that this compression happens before knowing the query. Without knowing which information will need to be recalled later, every window must be summarized in a ‘query-agnostic’ way. This structure gives rise to periodicity.
Toy Example: 8-Token Window, Stride 8Imagine a model with $S=8$. A new window starts at positions $0,8,16,\dots$. A token at position $t$ has phase $t \bmod 8$. That is, $t=0$ and $t=8$ both have phase $0$, and $t=1$ and $t=9$ both have phase $1$.
Now suppose the key-value pair “key: banana, value: yellow” is at position $t$. At retrieval, we throw in the query banana and must recover yellow.
If $t=7$, the key falls at the last offset of window $j$, and the value yellow falls at the first offset of the next window $j{+}1$. Since the key and value are split across the window boundary, both cannot fit inside a single compression entry. Intuitively, retrieval is difficult (source: §3). From $t=0$ to $t=6$, the key and value are inside the same window. And yet in experiments, accuracy differs by more than 50pp across these phases (source: §3). In other words, the boundary alone cannot explain the entire period. This dual asymmetry — “the case crossing the boundary vs. the difference that persists even inside the window” — is the analytical axis of this paper.
Gates Learn the PhaseThe clue to phase specialization lies in the gates. Because gate scores depend on the input, they can concentrate in two ways (source: §4).
Static concentration: whatever input arrives, the same offset is always preferred. → Fixed to a particular phase. Input-dependent concentration: the preferred offset changes with content. → Independent of phase. These two are distinguished by the effective number of offsets. Defined as $\exp(H(\alpha))$ for entropy $H$, it is $1$ for a one-hot and $W$ for a uniform distribution. Right after initialization, all gates are close to uniform ($\exp(H(\mathbb{E}[\alpha])) \approx 8$), but as pretraining proceeds, some heads slide down the diagonal and form static concentration (source: §4).
Specifically, in the reference model (W8/S8), the gates of layers 9, 10, and 14 form peaks at the late, middle, and early offsets of the window, respectively, and the value gates form peaks one offset after that. It looks as though a single head takes sole charge of a key-value pair (bigram) (source: §4). This peak phase exactly matches the phase where that head’s knockout loss is concentrated.
Performance Validation: Key ResultsThe Periodic Weakness of the DeepSeek-V4 FamilyThe most striking evidence is code completion. When DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base is asked to complete the type cast of its own inference code (an FP8 quantization function), a decorative docstring was prepended and only its length $L$ was varied from 24 to 39 tokens. The code is identical, yet the top-1 prediction flips periodically. The probability difference $P(8) - P(32)$ between the correct answer 8 and the wrong answer 32 oscillates from $-0.79$ to $+0.95$, and the flip repeats every 4 tokens (source: §2, Fig. headline). This period of 4 is exactly the stride $S=4$ of DeepSeek-V4 CSA. The same phenomenon appears with period 2 in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, whose stride is $S=2$, and in DeepSeek-V3.1-Base, which has no chunk compression, 32 comes out on top in only 4 of 64 inputs, so it effectively disappears (source: §2).
What systematizes this is a NIAH (needle-in-a-haystack) retrieval experiment at 128K context. 16k key-value pairs are inserted into a 128K-token prompt, and the original key value somewhere in the middle must be recovered (source: §2). Looking at accuracy by the remainder of the original key’s position divided by 8 (phase group), it reaches up to 40.2pp in the base checkpoint (source: §2, Fig. v4_niah). Although post-training raises accuracy and narrows the gap, the gap remains 19.14pp for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and 14.84pp for DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 (source: Tab. v4-niah-residue-accuracy). Even V4.1-Flash, with the smallest gap, is at 6.09pp, and all four even phase groups sit above all four odd groups (source: §2).
Controlled Pretraining: Confirming Compression Is the CauseDeepSeek-V4 differs from a standard transformer in many ways besides chunk compression, so one cannot retrain it without compression to check whether the periodicity disappears. So the authors pretrained from scratch a family of models using Qwen3-0.6B as the backbone, with KV compression as the sole architectural change. A total of 26 runs (23 compressed + 3 full-attention baselines) were trained to step 47,518 (source: §3, Tab. controlled-sweep-results).
The result is clear. Every compression model fluctuates periodically in line with the stride, and the full-attention baseline is flat (source: §3).
In particular, the period itself follows the stride. With window $W=8$ and strides $S\in\{4,6,8\}$, the periods are about 4, 6, and 8 tokens respectively, and about 12 tokens for $W{=}12/S{=}12$ (source: §3). And this phenomenon remains even without RoPE or learned gates. Replacing the gates with uniform mean pooling, or removing positional encoding, phase sensitivity persists (source: §3).
The most chilling number is ‘how much the average metric hides this difference.’ A W8/S8 compression model with 8 KV heads nearly approaches the full-attention baseline (61.1%) in average accuracy (59.4%) and validation loss, yet its worst phase-group accuracy is only 9.9%. The baseline’s lowest is 58.4% (source: §3, Tab. controlled-sweep-results). The Prefix Padding gap reaches up to 78pp in compression models, whereas the baseline is at most 6.1pp (source: §3).
This phenomenon is robust to seeds. Changing the seed changes the pattern of per-phase accuracy, but the periodic weakness itself reproduces across all seeds (source: Appx).
Mechanism: Phase SpecializationTo find the cause, KV head knockout was performed. The output of one head at a time is replaced with its mean across multiple prompts (mean replacement), erasing “the information specific to this prompt” (source: §4). In the full-attention baseline, the loss of each layer appears as horizontal stripes spread evenly across all phases. In compression models, by contrast, the loss is concentrated on particular phases, and each head shows a different phase-dependent pattern (source: §4, Fig. phase-knockouts). The same pattern repeats with a 4-token period in DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base as well.
Causality is then confirmed with a gate cycling intervention. Cycling the per-offset parameters of a statically concentrated gate by $k$ offsets shifts the accuracy pattern by roughly $k$ phases as well (source: §4). This shows that the learned gate preference is the cause of the per-phase retrieval asymmetry.
Theory: Why Gates Concentrate on PhaseFinally, the authors ask “why” with an idealized induction task. In a context where $LS$ tokens are divided into chunks of stride $S$, when a query repeats a token, the task is to predict its successor token (source: §5). Each head summarizes a chunk into a single compressed key/value. Two theorems follow (source: §5).
Theorem 1 (The optimal compression is concentrated). For a sufficiently large vocabulary $N$ and small error $\varepsilon$, the global minimizer concentrates the key weight on a single position $r$ and the value weight on $r{+}1$ as one-hots across all contexts, chunks, and heads. That is, even without knowing the query in advance, the loss prefers the most concentrated compression.
Theorem 2 (Gradient flow creates static concentration). Gradient flow starting from a small random initialization converges each head $h$ to a fixed position $r_h$, so that the key gate becomes a one-hot at $r_h$ and the value gate a one-hot at $r_h{+}1$. In Theorem 1 the chosen position could differ per input, but in Theorem 2 training fixes it per head.
This matches exactly the adjacent preference observed earlier in layers 9, 10, and 14 — “the key at a particular offset, the value at the next offset” (source: §5).
Our Perspective: Strengths, Limitations, and Why This MattersStrengths. The greatest value of this paper is that it cracks the inertia of ‘average accuracy.’ The fact that a periodic failure of up to 40pp can hide inside a model whose benchmark scores are the same has direct implications for the evaluation protocols of every long-context model that uses chunk compression. Methodologically it is clean too. It goes beyond manual observation of a single model and stacks four layers: (1) a large family of commercial models, (2) pretraining with a single controlled variable, (3) causal intervention, and (4) theoretical theorems. In particular, the experimental design of “shifting the input by a few tokens to change the phase of the same information” is easy to reproduce and could become a standard tool in this field.
Limitations. As the authors themselves state, the mechanistic conclusions are strongest in the controlled small-scale setting. They have not established a universal cause in large heterogeneous models (source: §7). A more important unresolved point is the duality. Since gate cycling cannot restore the boundary phase (the case where the key and value cross the window), it has not unified the boundary asymmetry and the within-window asymmetry into a single explanation (source: §7). The theory too is confined to the idealization of a bigram induction task and does not extend to the complex loss landscape of real pretraining. Many quantitative metrics are also concentrated on controlled tasks like NIAH and code completion, so the felt impact in real downstream applications remains open.
Why this matters. In long-context reasoning, where performance optimization is progressing rapidly, this paper pinpoints with concrete coordinates that “wherever you cut cost, a price hides somewhere.” Even a compression design that succeeds in raising the average can lose reliability depending on which phase the information lands in. This raises new questions for both evaluation methodology (phase-decomposed measurement rather than averages) and architecture design (phase homogenization).
What’s Next?: The Road AheadThe most practical task the authors leave behind is phase homogenization. Whether explicit coordination across heads and layers can even out per-phase retrieval quality, without sacrificing average performance or compression efficiency, remains open (source: §7).
In our view, the natural next steps are threefold.
Standardization of evaluation protocols. Add a procedure to existing long-context benchmarks (Lost in the Middle, RULER, etc.) that ‘shifts the input by $k$ tokens and measures per phase,’ and establish the practice of reporting the minimum and the gap alongside the average.
Exploring robustness implications. As the authors state, it is still unverified whether a meaning-preserving input shift changes response refusal or compliance, and whether that change tracks the compression phase (source: §7). The connection to safety-related behaviors such as prompt injection, jailbreaking, and consistency is an urgent question.
Design-level responses. If the static concentration of gates is one cause, it is worth experimenting with a loss term that regularizes it or derives a phase-independent compression operator, or with input preprocessing that mixes phases to spread out (pipeline) the weakness. The theoretical theorem says that “training naturally prefers concentration,” so simply training longer will not solve it.
Ultimately, the lesson this paper leaves is simple. The average is not an indicator of reassurance. When evaluating a model that uses chunk compression, one must ask not only for the average score but also how it fluctuates with phase.

content:
Paper MassAlloc Attention (MALA): Letting Attention Allocate Its Own Compute TL;DR — Full softmax attention (FullAttn) performs all post-score computation after QK score generation for every causal tile, whereas MALA uses the normalized mass produced by attention itself to selectively perform post-score operations. As a result, it maintains FullAttn-level quality while reducing training forward/backward latency by $2.2\times$ / $3.0\times$ and decoding latency by $1.6\times$, and cuts total training FLOPs by $23.1\%$ in 32K long-context training of a 14B model (source: Abstract, §3).
Core ideaBreaking attention computation into two stages makes the picture simpler.
Score discovery — the stage that multiplies $Q$ and $K$ to form $\mathbf{S}_{ij}=\mathbf{Q}_i\mathbf{K}_j^\top$. Post-score execution — everything after that. In forward, it is the softmax update, $V$ load, and $PV$ accumulation; in backward, it is probability reconstruction and the computation of $\mathrm{d}P$, $\mathrm{d}S$, $\mathrm{d}Q$, $\mathrm{d}K$, and $\mathrm{d}V$ (source: §2.1). FullAttn runs both stages for every legal causal tile without exception. But real attention distributions are highly non-uniform. Mass concentrates in local regions, sink tokens, and a small number of retrieval-relevant interactions, while most remaining interactions receive normalized mass small enough to ignore (source: §1). Yet dense kernels still process every low-contribution tile.
MALA’s central claim is this. Attention already produces scores and softmax statistics, so let that information decide which tiles deserve more computation. QK score access remains fully intact, and only post-score work is omitted for tiles with low normalized contribution.
That is, the authors hypothesize that “allocating post-score computation according to attention’s own normalized contribution can reduce training and inference cost while preserving operator fidelity, model quality, and long-range retrieval.”
Original Figure 1(fig:teaser). From left to right, it shows the forward and backward flows. Forward uses an evolving online softmax normalizer, while backward reuses the finalized normalizer saved by forward. The key point is that score discovery is retained for all tiles (source: §1, Fig. 1).
Background: The problem they solvedContext lengths are expanding from thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens. Long-document understanding, multi-turn reasoning, and repository-level code generation are driving this (source: §1). Attention over long contexts substantially increases computation and memory traffic.
FlashAttention greatly improved the IO efficiency of self-attention through tiling, fusion, and online softmax. But that improvement does not change the execution pattern itself. Every legal causal tile still performs all post-score computation once QK scores are produced (source: §1).
The structural limitations of prior methods identified in this paper fall into three broad categories (source: §1, §4).
Fixed sparse — uses support determined by position, such as local windows, structured blocks, and global tokens. Because it is position-based, it can misalign with the interactions the data actually needs. Dynamic sparse — selects tokens/blocks via content-based scores and routing. These can skip the QK computation for excluded interactions entirely, but require separate router, indexer, and mask state for selection. Adaptive top-p — chooses support adaptively against an estimated mass target. It estimates mass, and in some cases requires separate threshold calibration. The gap between them is where MALA sits. What if post-score computation were allocated inside the attention loop according to attention’s own normalized contribution? Preserve QK score access (cut only post-score) and build an efficient fused primitive for both training and inference. This is the research gap the paper explicitly addresses (source: §1, §2.4).
New approach: MassAlloc AttentionMALA reframes sparse attention as “distribution-conditioned compute allocation.” It summarizes three contributions (source: §1).
Formulation — keep every causal interaction score-accessible, and establish the view that the probability distribution produced by attention determines post-score work (§1). Implementation — a fused primitive that pairs an online forward rule with an offline backward rule and uses a common normalized-mass tolerance. It uses only standard attention state; forward has an omitted-mass upper bound, and backward has support nested within the forward support (§2.2, §2.4). Evaluation — six-stage validation: matched-work controlled experiments, operator fidelity, controlled associative recall, kernel execution, scaling-law training, and model-level evaluation (§3). The core design has three points.
One tolerance governs everythingDefine a common dimensionless tolerance $\tau$. Relative to the probability $1/L_q$ that uniform attention assigns to each key ($L_q$ is the number of causal keys query $q$ can see), form the length-aware threshold $\tau/L_q$. If a tile’s maximum contribution ratio is below this threshold, the tile is omitted (source: §2.1).
This single $\tau$ governs training forward, training backward, inference prefill, and autoregressive decoding. Across the experiments, the standard value $\tau=1$ is used (source: §3, §2.4). Because the threshold represents an allowed contribution, not a budget, sharp attention rows discard many tiles while diffuse rows keep more.
Forward: online sparse softmaxForward maintains the running maximum $\mathbf{m}_i$ and shifted normalizer sum $\ell_i$ of standard online softmax. The normalizer over the keys retained so far is
$$ Z_q^{(t)} = \sum_{k \in R_q^{(t)}} \exp(s_{qk}) = \exp\bigl(m_q^{(t)}\bigr)\,\ell_q^{(t)} $$and the maximum contribution ratio of a candidate tile is upper-bounded by
$$ r_{qj}^{(t)} = \frac{\exp\bigl(\max_{k \in J_j \cap \mathcal{C}_q} s_{qk}\bigr)}{Z_q^{(t)}} $$Because the denominator includes only the “mass retained so far”, this ratio can exceed 1, and it upper-bounds the dense-softmax probability of that tile. Taking logs yields the block-level test the kernel actually uses (source: §2.2):
$$ \operatorname{rowmax}(\mathbf{S}_{ij}) - \mathbf{m}_i - \log \ell_i < \log\!\bigl(\tau / \mathbf{L}_i\bigr) $$Omitted tiles leave $\mathbf{m}_i$, $\ell_i$, and the output accumulator $\mathbf{O}_i$ unchanged; only retained tiles perform the standard online-softmax update. The final output is therefore the same as ordinary softmax attention renormalized over the retained tiles (source: §2.2).
Backward: offline sparse probabilitiesBackward does not replay the sequence of partial normalizers from forward; it uses the final normalizer $Z_{R,q}$ saved by forward. Here “offline” means the normalizer is already finalized when tiles are examined, not that offline calibration is performed (source: §2.2).
In exact arithmetic, $Z_{R,q} \ge Z_q^{(t)}$, so using the final denominator cannot increase any key’s contribution ratio. Therefore, any tile omitted by forward is necessarily omitted by backward, and backward can additionally omit tiles that forward had retained while the normalizer was still incomplete. As a result, the backward support is nested within the forward support, achieved without storing a forward mask (source: §2.2).
An important nuance: this nesting does not guarantee the exact derivative of the forward operator. Backward may omit additional gradient contributions, and that error also depends on $\mathrm{d}O$ and $V$. Gradient fidelity is therefore measured directly at the operator level (source: §2.2).
Theoretical upper bound on forward omitted massProposition 1 in the appendix provides a quantitative guarantee of how safe forward is. For a query, let $Z_R$ be retained mass and $Z_O$ omitted mass; then the omitted probability mass is bounded by
$$ \epsilon_q = \frac{Z_O}{Z_R + Z_O} \le \frac{\tau}{1+\tau} $$With $\tau=1$, omitted mass can be as high as $50\%$ (a very loose bound), but measured values are orders of magnitude lower (source: Appendix §A.2, Prop. 1). Also, if the norm of value vectors is at most $V_{\max}$, output error is bounded by $\lVert o - \widetilde{o}\rVert \le \frac{2\tau}{1+\tau} V_{\max}$. This assumes exact arithmetic; in the finite precision of a fused implementation, rounding error must also be accounted for (source: Appendix §A.2).
How it works: a concrete exampleLet’s trace the abstract decision rule on a small input. (An illustrative example — unrelated to the paper’s experiments; it only demonstrates the mechanism.)
Suppose a single query sees four causal keys (positions $k_0, k_1, k_2, k_3$). Since $\tau=1$, the threshold is $\tau/L_q = 1/4 = 0.25$. Suppose $\exp(\text{score})$ for each key is as follows.
Key $\exp(s_k)$ Meaning $k_3$ (most recent) $e^2 \approx 7.39$ Recent token of medium strength $k_2$ $1$ Weak token $k_1$ (distant) $e^3 \approx 20.1$ Strong long-range token $k_0$ $1$ Weak token Forward traverses from the diagonal ($k_3$) toward the past. Tracking state changes step by step:
Step Tile $Z_q^{(t)}$ $r_{qj}^{(t)} = \frac{\exp(s)}{Z_q^{(t)}}$ Decision 1 $k_3$ 0 (first tile) $\infty$ keep (the first legal tile is always retained) 2 $k_2$ 7.39 $1/7.39 \approx 0.135$ omit ($0.135 < 0.25$) 3 $k_1$ 7.39 $20.1/7.39 \approx 2.72$ keep ($2.72 > 0.25$) 4 $k_0$ 27.49 $1/27.49 \approx 0.036$ omit ($0.036 < 0.25$) The final retained set is $\{k_3, k_1\}$, and the output is softmax renormalized over these two. Dense softmax would have given $k_0$ and $k_2$ about $3.4\%$ mass each, but MALA omits them. Two points matter. (1) Both the recent token ($k_3$) and the strong long-range token ($k_1$) are retained — locality is only a prior on execution order, not a support assumption. (2) Weak tokens fall below the threshold and are omitted.
In this 4-token example, omitted mass looks large at about $6.8\%$, but at realistic large-context scales $L_q$ is in the thousands to tens of thousands, so $\tau/L_q$ becomes extremely small and mass concentrates on a few tokens; the omitted mass reported in the paper falls to around $0.006\%$ (source: §3, Fig. 2). This example only shows which decisions occur in what order.
The same decision process repeats in backward, but backward uses the final normalizer ($27.49$) directly and can therefore be more selective than forward. For example, if forward retained a tile (at an early stage when the normalizer was still small), backward can omit it additionally (source: §2.2).
Performance validation: main resultsThe authors validate in six stages that ask progressively broader questions: allocation quality at fixed work → fidelity across context lengths → long-range association → kernel execution efficiency → quality-cost across model scales → full model evaluation (source: §3).
1) With equal work, allocation is decisiveThe most compelling experiment is the “matched-work” control. At 8K context, all policies perform exactly the same total post-score work (about 1,024 slots per query), and only how the work is distributed is compared (source: §3, Table 1).
Allocation scope Selection signal Mean omitted mass Mean output error Position only (position) Final reference mass 0.6012% 0.6231% Layer/head/position Final reference mass 0.1721% 0.2817% Input/layer/head/position (per-instance oracle) Final reference mass 0.0182% 0.0164% MALA (online mass upper bound) Online mass 0.0188% 0.0174% Moving from static allocation to per-input allocation (oracle) cuts omitted mass by $9.5\times$ and output error by $17.2\times$. MALA’s online test nearly matches this oracle (0.0188% vs. 0.0182%). In other words, the source of the gain is not “work” but “distribution-adaptive allocation” itself (source: §3, Table 1).
2) One tolerance holds across contextsRunning 1K–32K-token prefixes with the same $\tau=1$, forward work increases from 470 to 1,066 slots per query and backward from 462 to 1,058, then stabilizes at 1,010–1,066 after 8K. This stable range is why the experiments below use a reference of “about 1,024 slots.” Across all lengths, omitted mass is at most 0.0062% (P95 0.032%) and relative output error at most 0.021% (P95 0.14%). Gradient errors are within 0.38% for $\mathrm{d}Q$, 0.35% for $\mathrm{d}K$, and 0.17% for $\mathrm{d}V$ (source: §3, Fig. 2).
Original Figure 2(fig:operator_fidelity). The horizontal axis is context length (1K–32K); the top panel is mean post-score key slots per query; the bottom panel is relative error for omitted mass, output, and gradients. Even as context grows $32\times$, work flattens after 8K and error stays low — evidence for the claim that a single tolerance covers all lengths (source: §3, Fig. 2).
3) Long-range association is preservedOn controlled associative recall (256 key-value pairs), MALA tracks FullAttn closely as context grows. At sequence length 8,192 and $d_{model}=512$, MALA scores 89.67% vs. FullAttn 89.97%, while fixed-budget sparse methods collapse — DSA 52.61%, MoBA 47.25%, NSA 22.61% (source: §3, Fig. 3).
Original Figure 3(fig:ar). Panels are model dimensions ($d_{model}$=64–512); curves are accuracy versus sequence length (1,024–8,192). MALA stays close to the FullAttn curve, whereas fixed-budget (1,024 slots) sparse methods lose associations substantially as context grows. This supports the central claim that “support allocated by attention itself preserves associations that external selection or fixed support miss” (source: §3, Fig. 3).
4) Latency drops in real kernelsMeasured on 8 H100 GPUs with tensor parallelism $TP=8$ at 128K tokens. MALA reduces training forward latency by $2.2\times$, backward by $3.0\times$, and inference decoding by $1.6\times$ versus FullAttn. It has the lowest forward/backward latency among the compared methods, and its decoding is within 3% of DSA while being $1.6\times$ faster than FullAttn. Because allocation is fused into the attention loop and uses only standard attention state, peak memory remains at FullAttn’s level (source: §3, Fig. 4).
Original Figure 4(fig:latency_memory). The three panels show latency (left axis, bars) and per-rank peak memory (right axis, markers) for forward, backward, and decoding, respectively. FullAttn/MoBA/DSA/MALA are compared; MALA lowers latency while keeping peak memory at the same level as FullAttn. Measurements include the entire score-discovery and selection path of each method (source: §3, Fig. 4).
5) The quality-cost frontier shifts toward lower FLOPsIn scaling-law training at five scales from 0.6B to 14B, MALA tracks FullAttn’s perplexity closely while reducing total training FLOPs. At 14B, the perplexity difference is below 0.001 in both stages, while total FLOPs are reduced by $2.5\%$ in 4K pretraining and $23.1\%$ in 32K long-context training. The larger saving in long context occurs because MALA performs only the post-score work justified by the realized distribution while still including the full causal QK score-discovery cost (source: §3, Fig. 5).
Original Figure 5(fig:scaling_laws_flops). The left panel is the perplexity–FLOPs curve for 4K pretraining and the right for 32K long-context training. The FLOPs axis includes full score discovery and each method’s allocation/selection cost. The key point is that the MALA curve shifts left (lower cost) while tracking FullAttn closely — the gap widens especially in the 32K panel (source: §3, Fig. 5).
6) Model-level quality is preservedEvaluation summary for the final 14B model and for a 32B model trained further in a separate run (source: §3, Table 2).
Scale Method Knowledge Reasoning RULER 32K RULER 128K 14B FullAttn 72.32 64.46 89.42 65.84 14B MoBA 70.01 58.07 86.85 60.17 14B DSA 70.11 62.04 87.59 63.05 14B MALA 72.48 64.66 89.45 65.75 32B FullAttn 75.62 75.67 92.70 82.03 32B MALA 75.75 76.10 92.71 82.56 On average across knowledge, reasoning, 32K base retrieval, and YaRN-extrapolated 128K retrieval, MALA matches or slightly exceeds FullAttn at both scales. Notably, MoBA and DSA with a fixed budget fall substantially behind FullAttn at 14B (knowledge 70.01/70.11, reasoning 58.07/62.04), whereas MALA, which has no fixed budget, is on par with FullAttn (source: §3, Table 2, Appendix Tables 5–7).
Our perspective: strengths, limitations, and why this work mattersStrengthsThe paper’s greatest virtue is its experimental design that isolates causality. The matched-work control (Table 1) uses an oracle comparison to show that “the gain comes not from less work but from distribution-adaptive allocation”; operator fidelity (Fig. 2) independently verifies the tolerance’s generality; associative recall (Fig. 3) independently verifies preservation of long-range associations; kernel measurements (Fig. 4) independently verify real speedups; and scaling laws (Fig. 5) independently verify scalability. Each experiment fills a gap left by another.
On the design side it is also clean. A single $\tau$ spans training and inference, no separate mask, index, or router state is created, and forward omitted mass has an explicit upper bound (Prop. 1). The property that backward support is nested within forward support ensures consistency between the two passes without storage overhead (source: §2.4, Appendix §A.2).
LimitationsStart with the limitations the authors explicitly acknowledge.
QK complexity remains quadratic. The saving is only a data-dependent constant-factor reduction in post-score computation; score discovery is still performed in full (source: §2.3, §5). Support-sparse methods are complementary to MALA in that they can skip QK computation for excluded regions entirely. Backward is not the exact derivative of forward. Nesting does not guarantee an approximate derivative, so gradient fidelity is verified by measurement rather than theory (source: §2.2). The bound in Prop. 1 assumes exact arithmetic; in the finite precision of a fused implementation, rounding error is added (source: Appendix §A.2). As a reviewer, I would note the following potential limitations.
The sensitivity of $\tau=1$ was not validated. The claim is that a common tolerance works universally without separate calibration, but the main text has no ablation varying $\tau$. Unlike families such as Top-Theta that perform offline calibration, the optimality of insisting on a single constant remains open (source: §4). Absolute latency and cost are not reported. Only relative factors such as $2.2\times$/$3.0\times$/$1.6\times$ are given; there is no latency in ms or cost in dollars per 1M tokens. Actual savings depend on context length, distribution, and batch size, so absolute values under operating conditions are unverified (source: §3). The decoding saving ($1.6\times$) is smaller than the training savings ($2.2\times$/$3.0\times$). This appears to be because QK score discovery accounts for a larger share during single-token decoding. The benefit in latency-sensitive serving environments may not be as pronounced as in training. It does not touch the KV cache itself. MALA neither compresses nor evicts the cache; it keeps it intact, so savings in cache-capacity-bound scenarios are left to separate techniques (source: §2.4, §4). Why this work mattersWhereas prior efficient-attention work has mostly focused on which tokens/blocks to look at (support selection), MALA opens a complementary axis: look at all the scores, but choose which work to do afterward. These two axes are not mutually exclusive. Combining support sparsity, which reduces score discovery, with MALA, which reduces post-score work, could optimally reduce QK computation and post-score computation separately. In particular, the result that “FullAttn quality is maintained without a fixed budget” shows a way around the long-standing pain of tuning the budget hyperparameter in sparse attention (source: §1, §4).
What’s next?: The road aheadThe authors do not provide an explicit future-work list in the conclusion. Instead, in the related-work section they state that MALA “retains the full KV history for score discovery and value access, leaving cache storage and placement as separate optimization opportunities” (source: §4, §5). Combining this direction with the limitations above suggests the following reasonable next steps.
Reduce QK discovery too — combine with support-sparse methods (MoBA, DSA, etc.). Reducing the quadratic cost of score discovery while preserving post-score savings is the next bottleneck for long-context scalability. Automatic/offline calibration of $\tau$ — go beyond validating a single constant’s generality and measure the quality-cost Pareto frontier when $\tau$ is calibrated per layer, head, and context length. Validate absolute serving metrics — report absolute decoding latency (ms/token), TTFT, and batch scalability to confirm benefits from an operational rather than training-centric perspective. Longer contexts (1M+) and other modalities — YaRN 128K extrapolation has already been verified, but test whether the same normalized-mass allocation holds for native ultra-long contexts and vision/multimodal attention. Combine with KV cache management — add compression/eviction techniques on top of the full KV cache that MALA retains, covering cache-capacity-bound scenarios as well. The idea of letting attention allocate its own computation is simple, but it is presented with a cumulative six-stage experimental design, symmetric forward/backward rules, and a theoretical upper bound, making it highly convincing. The source is available at HKUSTDial/flash-sparse-attention (source: Abstract).

title: MassAlloc Attention: Let Attention Allocate Its Own Compute

content:
Paper WorldAttention: System Co-Design of an Interactive Video World Model That Drops the Sliding WindowTL;DR — Text-controlled interactive video world models are trapped between the demand to “remember the entire history” and the reality that “the KV cache grows linearly until GPU memory blows up.” Researchers at Alibaba DAMO Academy solve this dilemma with an attention architecture called WorldAttention. A hierarchical KV cache (HKV) splits memory into pages and distributes them across a multi-tier memory hierarchy, a hybrid sparse attention (HSA) makes the computation linear and sparse, and custom kernels push actual hardware performance to the limit. The results are a VBench-Long subject consistency of 0.9472, an InterVBench score of 0.9668, and 22.0 FPS on a single H100 GPU (source: Abstract, Tab. 1).
Core IdeaThe essential difficulty of interactive long video generation lies in prompt switching. When the user says “throw that red ball again” after about 50 seconds, the model must recall detailed visual information from tens of seconds earlier (source: §1 Introduction). For this reason, a plain sliding window is unsuitable because it “discards the past entirely,” while keeping the full-history KV instead causes memory to blow up linearly (source: §1 Introduction).
WorldAttention’s answer has three prongs (source: Fig. 1):
HKV (Hierarchical KV Cache) — splits past KV into “pages” of 8 frames and places them across GPU SRAM/HBM → CPU DRAM → NVMe, retrieving only the needed pages via two-stage search. HSA (Hybrid Sparse Attention) — combines a linear attention branch and a head-adaptive block sparse branch to reduce quadratic complexity to effectively linear and sparse levels. Custom kernels — reorganize retrieved pages into a contiguous buffer to eliminate the hardware waste caused by non-contiguous memory access. The paper’s core insight is that these three elements must mesh organically to deliver real speed. Interestingly, the authors demonstrate head-on through experiments that “kernel optimization alone is not enough” (source: Tab. 9).
Background: The Problem They SolvedText-conditioned interactive video world models aim to simulate a temporally consistent environment that responds to user prompts, built on the autoregressive diffusion paradigm (source: Abstract). Enabling low-latency, long-horizon generation here is key to embodied AI and simulation-based planning, but existing frameworks were trapped in a trade-off between two broad directions (source: §1 Introduction).
Sliding-window KV cache (MAGI-1, Self Forcing, LongLive, SkyReels-V2, CausVid, etc.) saves GPU memory by keeping only recent tokens, but it permanently discards visual context from tens of seconds earlier (source: §2 Related Work). When the user refers to an earlier scene, the required visual details are already gone.
Sparse-retrieval KV cache (BIFE) preserves the entire history to support recall, but the KV cache grows linearly with video length and soon exceeds GPU memory capacity (source: §2 Related Work). Moreover, BIFE’s retrieval unit is the chunk level, so even when only some tokens are actually relevant, the whole chunk is loaded (source: §3.1 HKV).
In other words, the gap the paper attacks is the absence of an attention architecture that satisfies both “full-history memory” and “efficient management.” The authors fill it with a system co-design along two axes: “attention redesign + hierarchical caching mechanism” (source: §1 Introduction).
New Approach: WorldAttentionWorldAttention is built on the Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B backbone and generates 5-second clips at 16 FPS and 480p (832×480) resolution (source: §4.2 Implementation). Let us take the core design apart piece by piece.
HKV: Page-Level Multi-Tier MemoryHKV refines the existing “chunk-level” KV management into finer “page-level” units. Each page holds 8 consecutive frames, and one frame is 1,560 tokens (source: §3.1 HKV). Memory is organized into 4 tiers (source: §3.1 HKV):
L0 (GPU SRAM) — on-chip memory where Q·K·V are computed in FlashAttention style L1 (GPU HBM) — retrieved KV pages + prompt/page indices L2 (CPU DRAM) — KV chunks not used in the current chunk generation L3 (NVMe) — the final backup of all KV chunks By aligning access frequency with hardware bandwidth, frequently used pages stay on the GPU and less-used chunks are automatically offloaded to the CPU. As a result, no matter how large the total KV grows, GPU (L1) occupancy stays bounded (source: §3.1 HKV, Fig. 2).
Retrieval happens in two stages (source: §3.1 HKV):
Prompt stage — selects the top-1 chunk by cosine similarity between the current prompt embedding and the prompt embeddings of past chunks. Page stage — selects the top-$K_p$ pages using the score $\alpha_{m,j} = \frac{\bar{Q}^\top \bar{K}_{m,j}}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ between the current chunk’s mean query $\bar{Q}$ and each page’s mean key $\bar{K}_{m,j}$ (where $K_p = 4$). The final active KV is $4 \times 8 \times 1560 = 49{,}920$ tokens. Prompt retrieval narrows the search space, and page retrieval picks out fine-grained context — a complementary structure (source: §4.5 Ablations).
HSA: Dual Branches of Linear + SparseBecause spatiotemporal redundancy remains even in retrieved pages, HSA allocates computation more finely across two branches (source: §3.2 HSA).
The linear branch uses Linformer-style low-rank projections. For each head $h$, it compresses keys and values with learned projection matrices $\mathbf{E}_K^{(h)}, \mathbf{E}_V^{(h)} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times r}$:
$$ \widetilde{\mathbf{K}}^{(h)} = (\mathbf{E}_K^{(h)})^\top \mathbf{K}^{(h)}, \quad \widetilde{\mathbf{V}}^{(h)} = (\mathbf{E}_V^{(h)})^\top \mathbf{V}^{(h)} $$This reduces complexity from $\mathcal{O}(L^2 d_k)$ to $\mathcal{O}(L r d_k)$. Since the projection rank $r \ll L$ is fixed, it is linear in $L$ (source: §3.2 HSA). The authors point out that the approach of existing linear attention (SLA, etc.) — “compressing an infinite past into a fixed-size hidden state” — causes memory superposition and attention dilution, and argue that Linformer’s explicit structural downsampling preserves spatiotemporal physical anchors (source: Appx. Linear Branch).
The sparse branch performs block-level sparse computation at the original token resolution. It divides retrieved pages into blocks of size $B$, performs coarse block selection with a pooled attention map, and then runs SDPA with a block-sparse kernel only on the selected blocks (source: §3.2 HSA). The block size is set to a multiple of 16, the MMA/WGMMA compute unit on Hopper. It uses $B_{\text{inter}}=128$ for past pages (inter-chunk) and $B_{\text{intra}}=64$ for current chunk tokens (intra-chunk) (source: §3.2 HSA).
Head-adaptive sparsity is the charm of this branch. Instead of a fixed Top-K, each head determines its own sparsity level from the Gini coefficient $\mathcal{G}^{(h)}$ of its attention distribution (source: Appx. Sparse Branch):
$$ \tau_h = \tau_{\min} + \mathcal{G}^{(h)} \cdot (\tau_{\max} - \tau_{\min}) $$For each head, it selects only the minimal set of blocks whose cumulative attention mass exceeds the threshold $\tau_h$. Heads with peaked distributions (focused on local interactions) and uniform heads (broad context) operate with different sparsity, which is finer-grained than layer- or globally fixed sparsity (source: §3.2 HSA, Fig. 3).
The two branches are fused by a per-head multiplicative gate:
$$ \mathbf{O}^{(h)} = \mathbf{O}^{(h)}_{\text{lin}} \odot \mathbf{G}^{(h)}_{\text{lin}} + \mathbf{O}^{(h)}_{\text{sp}} \odot \mathbf{G}^{(h)}_{\text{sp}} $$The linear branch ensures global information flow, while the sparse branch handles high-resolution modeling where needed (source: §3.2 HSA).
How It Works: A Concrete ExampleLet us follow the whole process through one of the paper’s visualization examples, the “Rio’s Christmas street” scene (source: Appx. Visualization). Suppose it is a 60-second video in which a man in a blue shirt throws a red ball, followed by a ribbon and then a flaming torch.
1. Chunk splitting and KV bank initialization. The 60-second video is generated as 12 five-second chunks. Each chunk’s KV is split into pages $\mathcal{P}_{m,j}$ of 8 frames and stored in the global KV bank $\mathcal{B}$ (source: §3.1 HKV).
2. A prompt switch occurs. In the 50–60 second segment, the user requests “that man throws the red ball again.” The model must recall the red ball scene from the 10–20 second segment.
3. Two-stage retrieval. First, the current prompt embedding is compared with each chunk’s prompt embedding to pick the 10–20 second chunk as top-1. Then, within that chunk, the top-4 pages are selected by similarity between the current mean query and each page’s mean key. As a result, the active KV becomes $4 \times 8 \times 1560 = 49{,}920$ tokens and is loaded into L1 (GPU HBM) (source: §3.1 HKV).
4. HSA computation. These 49,920 tokens enter both branches. Assuming $L = 49{,}920$, $d_k = 128$, and $r = 64$, the linear branch operates at roughly $L r d_k \approx 4.1 \times 10^8$ versus full attention’s $QK^\top$ at $L^2 d_k \approx 3.2 \times 10^{11}$ FLOPs — about $L/r \approx 780\times$ less along the dimension axis. The sparse branch filters blocks by a Gini-coefficient-based threshold, actually computing only the high-mass blocks.
5. Gate fusion and output. The two branch outputs are mixed by per-head gates to drive denoising of the current chunk. This process repeats for each chunk, keeping the entire 60 seconds consistent.
The overall flow can be summarized in a diagram:
flowchart TD A[Prompt + current chunk] --> B[Generate query tokens] C[Global KV Bank<br/>past chunks = pages] --> D[Stage 1: prompt retrieval<br/>Top-1 chunk] D --> E[Stage 2: page retrieval<br/>Top-4 pages] E --> F[Active KV 49,920 tokens<br/>load into L1 GPU HBM] B --> G[HSA] F --> G subgraph G[HSA hybrid sparse attention] G1[Linear branch<br/>Linformer low-rank] G2[Sparse branch<br/>head-adaptive block sparse] end G1 --> H[Gate fusion] G2 --> H H --> I[Current chunk output] Performance Validation: Key ResultsQuality: Best on Every Metric on VBench-LongOn the VBench-Long benchmark extended to 60 seconds, WorldAttention set the best score on most metrics with subject consistency 0.9472, background consistency 0.9691, motion smoothness 0.9915, dynamic degree 0.7758, and image quality 0.7259 (source: Tab. 1). That is +0.0062 over the previous best, BIFE (subject consistency 0.9410), and a clear improvement over LongLive (0.9403).
Its quality score of 85.53 over the full 60 seconds beats SkyReels-V2 (80.49), Self-Forcing (82.46), BIFE (84.38), and LongLive (83.95) (source: Tab. 2). The per-segment CLIP scores also stay at the top overall, from 0–10 seconds (29.04) to 50–60 seconds (25.01), showing little identity drift even after a prompt switch (source: Tab. 2).
Quality: Drift Metrics on InterVBenchOn InterVBench, a chunk-level long-horizon generation benchmark, WorldAttention recorded the lowest (least drift) VDE subject 0.0792, VDE background 0.2850, VDE motion 0.0095, and VDE clearness 0.7390, while achieving subject consistency 0.9668, background consistency 0.9614, and motion smoothness 0.9972 (source: Appx. InterVBench). This means it shows the least blurring or shaking over time.
Efficiency: 14.02× Kernel, 22 FPS on a Single GPUEfficiency is the highlight of this paper. The custom kernel HSA_tk (built on ThunderKittens) shows a 14.02× speedup over FlashAttention-3, and the end-to-end speedup when combined with HKV is 2.21× (source: Abstract, §4.3 Efficiency). On a single H100, it maintains 22.0 FPS while reaching a quality score of 86.55, capturing both quality and speed (source: Tab. 3). This surpasses Self-Forcing (17.0 FPS), BIFE (18.0 FPS), and LongLive (20.7 FPS).
Decomposing the end-to-end speedup by stage, it accumulates as HKV (+1.15×) → HSA (+1.91×) → kernel customization (+2.21×) (source: Tab. 9). On the B200 GPU as well, it reaches 2.46× for a 14B model at 720p and 60 seconds, and 2.35× for the 90-second setting, so the gains grow with longer sequences and larger models (source: Tab. 10).
Secret Weapon: Why This Combination?The ablation study that carved out HSA’s design space is striking (source: Tab. 4):
Configuration Subject consistency Dynamic degree Image quality Linear branch only 0.9021 0.5825 0.6490 Sparse only (τ=1.00/0.35) 0.9365 0.6945 0.6995 Linear+sparse (τ=0.75/0.35) 0.9300 0.7520 0.7015 Linear+sparse (τ=1.00/0.35) 0.9472 0.7758 0.7259 The two branches are complementary. The linear branch is strong on subject and background consistency but weak on motion dynamics and visual quality, while the sparse branch is the opposite. Combined, every metric rises (source: §4.5 Ablations). In an analysis comparing the linear branch with SLA, SANA-Video, and full attention, the Linformer approach restored the long-range mass distribution of full attention most faithfully and also had the highest output cosine similarity (source: Fig. 4).
The HKV retrieval design is validated as well. Under the same 4-page budget, HKV (85.53) overwhelms recent-page retrieval (83.74), random retrieval (82.86), and mismatched retrieval (80.96), and the gap widens especially in the 50–60 second CLIP score, at 25.01 vs 21.48/20.12/17.36 (source: Tab. 7). It also shows robustness: even when three semantically similar chunks are mixed in, quality barely drops from 85.53 to 85.18 (source: Tab. 8).
Our Take: Strengths, Limitations, and Why This Work MattersStrengthsThe biggest contribution is that it proves with data that “algorithm-hardware co-design is essential.” Decomposing HSA execution time, the sparse attention kernel itself accounts for only 1.86% of the total, while KV reconstruction and contiguous memory copying take 31.00% and the linear branch takes 39.78% (source: Tab. 9). In other words, optimizing only the kernel misses the bottleneck. This is the real insight of a systems paper, directly refuting the conventional wisdom that “the optimal kernel = the best performance.”
Second, the page-level two-stage retrieval is simple yet effective. Using prompt retrieval to keep retrieval cost independent of sequence length and page retrieval to obtain fine-grained context is a complementary structure (source: §4.5) that is clean from an engineering standpoint.
Third, the consistency of the results. The same conclusion emerges across two benchmarks (VBench-Long and InterVBench), two axes (quality and efficiency), two hardware platforms (H100 and B200), and two scales (1.3B and 14B) (source: Tab. 10).
LimitationsThe limitation the authors explicitly acknowledge is that it uses only text prompts as the control signal. It cannot handle richer conditional modalities such as action signals, control trajectories, or embodied interaction cues (source: Appx. Limitation).
Several potential limitations are also apparent. First, the setting in which training samples contain exactly one prompt switch may underestimate real multi-turn, multi-event interactions (source: §4.2 Implementation). The paper itself admits that “top-1 chunk retrieval may be unsuitable for multi-event prompts” (source: §4.5). Second, hyperparameters such as the page size (8 frames) and $K_p=4$ are fixed, so adapting to content density remains future work. Third, the backbone is small at 1.3B, so whether the gains remain linear on larger DiTs is not fully proven by the single 14B setting alone.
Why It MattersThis work brings the central problem of LLM serving — KV cache management — into the entirely different domain of video generation, systematically dismantling the fundamental tension between “full memory” and “bounded memory.” At a time when low-latency, long-horizon interactive generation is becoming increasingly important in embodied AI and simulation-based planning, this framework offers a reusable design pattern.
What’s Next?: The Road AheadThe direction the authors propose is action-conditioned generation. Integrating action signals would enable controllable environment simulation and decision-making-based video prediction beyond a plain text-to-video model, allowing it to evolve into a true “video world model” (source: Appx. Limitation).
Adding reasonable next steps on top of this:
Support for multi-event, multi-turn switching. It is natural to relax the top-1 chunk assumption and adaptively allocate the retrieval budget according to prompt complexity. Adaptive page size. A density-adaptive strategy that splits segments with frequent scene changes into smaller pages and static segments into larger pages. Large-backbone validation. Verification is needed of how HKV’s offload policy and HSA’s sparsity gains scale on 7B/14B-class DiTs. Energy- and cost-oriented evaluation. Quantifying the power and latency cost of the multi-tier memory (especially NVMe round trips) would clarify the real-serving trade-offs. In the end, the paper’s message is clear. The bottleneck of interactive long-horizon generation lies not in any single layer but at the interface between attention structure, memory management, and hardware execution, and only when that interface is co-designed does a system emerge that “keeps both the memory and the speed.”

title: WorldAttention: An Efficient Attention Architecture for Interactive Video World Models

content:
Paper PISA: Pyramid Top-$K$ Selection Lowers the Cost of Block-Sparse Attention to $O(N\log N)$ TL;DR — Block-sparse attention makes attention computation linear, but block selection still costs quadratic time. PISA solves this by layering keys into a pyramid via average pooling and narrowing candidates at each level with LogSumExp (LSE) scores. Prefill selection cost drops to $O(N\log N)$ and decode to $O(\log N)$, delivering up to $9.95\times$ speedup in selection latency over existing BSA at 256K tokens.
Key IdeaPISA (Pyramid Sparse Attention) redesigns Top-$K$ block selection, the bottleneck among the two stages of block-sparse attention. Existing block-sparse attention (BSA) scores every query–block pair and then picks the top $K$; this stage alone costs $O(N^2/C)$ (source: §1). PISA stratifies key blocks via average pooling to narrow candidates at a coarse level and expand only the selected candidates to a finer level (source: §3.2). Because the number of candidates evaluated at each level is bounded, selection costs $O(\log N)$ per query and total prefill drops to $O(N\log N)$ (source: §3.4, Table 1).
There are three core design choices. ① Pyramid hierarchy: keys are aggregated bottom-up with block size $C=64$ and branching factor $g=2$. ② LSE scoring: instead of approximating candidate blocks with a simple mean or mean+variance, it scores them with the exact LSE, $\log\sum\exp(\cdot)$. ③ Hardware-aware kernels: hierarchical routing and LSE scoring are fused into a single Triton kernel; training/prefill use a two-stage kernel and decode uses a one-stage kernel (source: §3.3, Algorithm 1).
Background: The Problem They SolvedThe cost of self-attention grows quadratically with sequence length $N$, blocking scaling to long contexts (source: §1). Block-sparse attention sidesteps this by restricting each query to a selected subset of key blocks rather than all keys. Grouping into blocks enables tiled kernels, which is efficient (source: §1).
Block-sparse attention splits into two stages (source: §3.1):
Top-$K$ block selection — each query decides which key blocks to attend to Attention computation over the selected blocks — using the original keys/values The problem lies in stage 1, not stage 2. Because each query attends to at most $KC$ keys, attention computation is linear in the sequence, but the selection stage still requires every query to scan every key block, leaving it at $O(N^2/C)$ (source: §1, §3.1). In other words, this paper identifies selection as the real bottleneck in long-context modeling—the research gap it targets.
The authors clearly position their work here. Existing hierarchical methods such as HiP are training-free, while trainable methods such as NSA and HiLS still have $O(N^2)$ prefill complexity. PISA is the only method that is trainable while achieving both $O(N\log N)$ prefill and $O(\log N)$ decode (source: Table 1, §2).
New Approach: PISA (Pyramid Sparse Attention)3.1 Building the Key-Block PyramidThe key-block hierarchy is built fine-to-coarse (source: §3.2). Level $0$ consists of singleton blocks of the original keys, level $1$ consists of leaf blocks of size $C=64$, and each subsequent level is formed by concatenating $g=2$ adjacent child blocks. The summary vector $\bar{k}_i^{(\ell)}$ of each block is computed recursively by average pooling over its child summaries:
$$ \bar{k}_i^{(\ell+1)} = \frac{1}{|\operatorname{Ch}_\ell(i)|} \sum_{r\in\operatorname{Ch}_\ell(i)} \bar{k}_r^{(\ell)} $$where $\operatorname{Ch}_\ell(i)$ is the set of child indices of block $i$ at level $\ell$ (source: §3.2, Eq. mean_pyramid). Because this is downsampling, the number of levels is $L=O(\log N)$ (source: §3.4).
3.2 Selection from Coarse to Fine LevelsSelection starts at the coarsest level $L$ and descends to leaf level $1$ (source: §3.2). At each level $\ell$:
Compute LSE scores $\mathbf{s}_t^{(\ell)}$ for the candidate set $\mathcal{A}_t^{(\ell)}$ Keep only the top-$K$ blocks $\mathcal{I}_t^{(\ell)}$ Form the candidate set $\mathcal{A}_t^{(\ell-1)}$ for the next level from the children of the selected blocks Since each selected block has at most $g$ children, the number of candidates at the next level is bounded by $gK$ (source: §3.2, Eq. candidate_bound). This is the key to reducing quadratic cost to log-linear.
3.3 LSE Scoring: Why LSE Instead of a Simple MeanThe score of candidate block $K_i^{(\ell)}$ is defined as the exact LogSumExp over its child summaries (source: §3.2):
$$ s_{t,i}^{(\ell)} = \log\sum_{r\in\operatorname{Ch}_{\ell-1}(i)} \exp\!\left(\frac{q_t^\top \bar{k}_r^{(\ell-1)}}{\sqrt{d}}\right) $$The authors justify this choice with a Taylor expansion. For the mean $\bar{z}$ and variance $\operatorname{Var}(z)$ of $z_1,\dots,z_m$, the LSE expands as follows (source: §4.4, Appendix A):
$$ \log\sum_{j=1}^{m}e^{z_j} = \log m + \bar z + \tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(z) + \text{higher-order terms} $$In other words, the two variants the authors compare are truncated versions of this expansion (source: §4.4):
PISA-1: first-order approximation → uses only the mean $\bar{z}$ PISA-2: second-order approximation → uses $\bar{z} + \tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(z)$ PISA (this method): no truncation; uses the full LSE According to the Jensen-inequality analysis in Appendix A, scoring an intermediate block by the LSE of its child means is always closer to the original-key LSE than the mean of child means (PISA-1) (source: Appendix A).
3.4 Hardware-Aware KernelsPISA lets query heads within a GQA group share the same key blocks, and handles training/prefill and decode with different kernels (source: §3.3, Algorithm 1):
Training/prefill — two-stage kernel: stage 1 performs hierarchical selection at intermediate levels, and stage 2 scores the original key blocks. In stage 2, queries are grouped into tiles ($Q_{\mathrm{tile}}=4$) so that multiple queries reuse the same key blocks, reducing IO. With $G_Q=16$ and $C=64$, $G_Q + C/Q_{\mathrm{tile}} = 32 < 64 = C$, so leaf-level IO is lower than with a single stage (source: §3.4). Decode — one-stage kernel: decode has only one query, so there is no cross-query reuse; to avoid the overhead of launching multiple kernels, it processes all the way to $\ell=1$ in a single kernel. It caches the average pyramid and updates only the current leaf average and the ancestor path for each new token (source: §3.3, Appendix B). Throughout the process, the query–key score matrix is never materialized, which is a strength in terms of memory traffic (source: §1).
How It Works: A Concrete Example The following is an illustrative example for intuition; the numbers are scaled down and unrelated to the paper’s actual experimental settings ($C=64$, $K=8/32$, $g=2$).
Suppose there are keys $k_1,\dots,k_{16}$, block size $C=4$, and branching factor $g=2$. The pyramid has three levels.
flowchart TB subgraph L2["Level 2 (coarsest)"] R["root: [k1..k16]"] end subgraph L1["Level 1 (middle)"] P1["P1: [k1..k8]"] P2["P2: [k9..k16]"] end subgraph L0["Level 1 leaves (C=4)"] B1["B1: [k1..k4]"] B2["B2: [k5..k8]"] B3["B3: [k9..k12]"] B4["B4: [k13..k16]"] end R --> P1 & P2 P1 --> B1 & B2 P2 --> B3 & B4 With a block budget of $K=1$, selection proceeds as follows (source: §3.2, Eq. hierarchical_topk).
Step Level Candidate set $\mathcal{A}$ Scored Result Initialization 2 {root} (skipped since candidates ≤ K) root kept Expansion 2→1 {P1, P2} Score P1 and P2 by the LSE of their child summaries P1 selected Expansion 1→leaf {B1, B2} Score B1 and B2 by the exact LSE of the original keys B1 selected Attention — {B1} — Attend only to keys $k_1..k_4$ The key point is that at each level, only the candidates that survived the previous level are scored, not the entire set. As we descend, the number of blocks doubles, but the number of blocks scored is fixed at at most $gK$ (source: §3.2). Therefore, even as the sequence grows and the number of levels increases to $O(\log N)$, the number of scores computed per query stays at $O(\log N)$.
An important nuance is that intermediate levels use the LSE of summaries, while the leaf level uses the LSE of the original keys. Scoring an intermediate block against all original keys would itself be quadratic, so it approximates with summaries and reads the original keys exactly only at the final leaves (source: §3.2, Appendix A).
Performance Validation: Main ResultsExperiments train decoder-only backbones at three scales—418M, 1.47B, and 2.67B—from scratch on 100B tokens @ 4K, then continue pretraining (CPT) on 10B tokens @ 16K. Sparse methods share block size $C=64$, with block budgets of $K=8$ for pretraining and $K=32$ for CPT (source: §4.1).
5.1 Language Modeling and Downstream PerformanceAfter training from scratch (100B @ 4K), PISA is on par with BSA, NSA, and HiLS in language modeling and commonsense reasoning, and its average accuracy on six containment (retrieval) tasks is the highest among sparse methods at all three scales (source: §4.2, Table 2). However, Full Attention still has a higher average (source: §4.2).
Scale PISA loss ↓ BSA loss ↓ Containment avg (PISA) Containment avg (BSA) 418M 2.5630 2.5684 41.77 38.18 1.47B 2.3162 2.3179 49.83 48.54 2.67B 2.2151 2.2184 52.14 51.13 Lower loss and higher accuracy are better. Numbers excerpted from Table 2 (§4.2).
These results support the claim that “hierarchical selection reduces computational complexity while preserving the blocks needed for downstream modeling” (source: §1, §4.2).
5.2 Long-Context Retrieval (RULER)After CPT (16K), the 2.67B model was evaluated on RULER’s four needle-in-a-haystack task groups. PISA led with an average accuracy of 62.80, ahead of BSA (54.99) and NSA (61.07); the PISA-2 variant was best among sparse methods at 62.92 (source: Table 3, §4.3).
In particular, PISA showed the best accuracy among sparse methods on multi-key (1K/2K) and multi-value (1K/2K/4K), but at longer lengths of 8K/16K, NSA led on single-key and multi-key tasks (source: Table 3). In other words, PISA’s strength is concentrated in specific tasks and lengths rather than across the entire long-context regime.
5.3 Block Selection Quality (Oracle Diagnosis)All selectors were replayed with the queries and keys from a Full-Attention checkpoint to measure how well they match the actual full-attention mass (source: §4.4, Appendix D). For $K=8$:
Selector Recall@8 ↑ Captured mass ↑ Attention mass ratio ↑ BSA 85.91 85.67 98.42 PISA-1 (mean) 84.75 85.50 98.22 PISA-2 (mean+variance) 88.24 86.13 99.02 PISA (LSE) 90.95 86.47 99.46 PISA is best on all three metrics, and the selected blocks recover 99.46% of the mass contained in the full-attention reference (source: §4.4, Appendix D). This is direct evidence that LSE scoring produces more accurate Top-$K$ selection. Interestingly, PISA-1 (simple mean) is even lower than BSA, showing that “score accuracy” translates into actual performance differences.
5.4 Selection Latency (Kernel Microbenchmark)Prefill block-selection latency was measured from 4K to 256K (source: §4.5, Table 6/Appendix B). The most important insight here is that BSA is faster at short lengths.
$N$ BSA (ms) PISA Q4 (ms) BSA speed vs. PISA 4K 0.167 0.701 BSA $4.2\times$ faster 16K 1.461 1.581 BSA faster 32K 5.099 3.185 PISA faster 64K 19.144 6.704 PISA $2.86\times$ 128K 76.682 14.452 PISA $5.31\times$ 256K 312.956 31.441 PISA $9.95\times$ Numbers excerpted from Appendix B (Table, kernel_grouped_benchmark) and the text in §4.5. Batch 1, 32 query heads, 2 KV heads, $d=64$, $C=64$, $K=8$, $g=2$, BF16.
This crossover summarizes the paper’s core message. PISA’s advantage is asymptotic. Because of constant overhead (hierarchy construction, multi-stage expansion), BSA leads at 16K and below, but as length grows, BSA’s $O(N^2)$ selection becomes exponentially slower, while PISA’s $O(N\log N)$ grows gently (source: §4.5).
Our Perspective: Strengths, Limitations, and Why This Work MattersStrengthsThe biggest contribution is reframing the problem precisely. Whereas prior block-sparse literature focused on the quadratic cost of attention computation, PISA points out that “the selection stage itself remains a bottleneck at $O(N^2/C)$” and attacks that bottleneck directly (source: §1). The second strength is the justification for LSE scoring. It does not merely use LSE; it provides theoretical support via a Taylor expansion and Jensen’s inequality for why it is superior to mean and mean+variance approximations (source: §4.4, Appendix A). The third is engineering honesty. The authors explain the split into a two-stage training/prefill kernel and a one-stage decode kernel via an inequality on leaf-level Q/K IO cost, and they do not hide the fact that BSA is faster at short lengths (source: §3.4, §4.5).
Limitations: What the Authors AcknowledgeThe authors explicitly acknowledge that model scale and pretraining data budget were limited by compute constraints, and note that this may affect performance and relative gains over baselines (source: Appendix E, Limitations). In practice, experiments stop at a 2.67B model and 100B tokens, leaving open whether the gains hold for production LLMs at tens to hundreds of billions of parameters.
Limitations: A Reviewer’s ReasoningSeveral points warrant caution.
Constant overhead and the crossover point. PISA is slower than BSA at 16K and below (source: §4.5). Which is better in real serving contexts (typically 4K–128K) is sensitive to the crossover location, and this crossover depends on hardware and kernel implementation. Size of the performance advantage. It is “on par” in language modeling and commonsense reasoning; clear advantages are concentrated in containment average (best among sparse) and selection-quality metrics (source: §4.2). Even in long-context RULER, NSA leads on certain 8K/16K tasks (source: Table 3). In other words, it is an advantage under specific conditions, not across the board. Approximation in GQA group scoring. The authors themselves note that summing query-head LSEs and averaging full-attention mass can yield different rankings (source: Appendix A, gqa_objective). This is a source of theoretical mismatch. Pyramid cache cost. Decode caches the average pyramid and doubles the buffer each time length doubles, with total copy cost $O((N/C)d\log N)$ (source: Appendix B). The average remains $O(\log N)$, but the fact that this cache occupies VRAM separately from the KV cache must be considered in inference-time memory accounting. Why This Work MattersUltimately, PISA is progress that lowers the complexity of the “selection stage of sparse attention” by one level. Among trainable methods, it achieves both $O(N\log N)$ prefill and $O(\log N)$ decode, and that complexity is implemented in real kernels and validated with a $9.95\times$ speedup at 256K (source: Table 1, §4.5)—meaningfully pushing the bottleneck of long-context modeling further back.
What’s Next?: The Road AheadThe authors do not explicitly propose future directions, but given the limitations, reasonable next steps are as follows.
Scale validation: most urgent is to verify whether the gains and quality loss of $O(N\log N)$ selection hold at 7B+ and multi-trillion-token scale (source: connected to the limitations discussion in Appendix E). Move the crossover earlier: kernel optimization to reduce the constant overhead (hierarchy construction, multi-stage expansion) in the 4K–16K range where PISA is slower than BSA, bringing the advantage in practical contexts forward. Inference-serving integration: follow-up work quantifying the VRAM overhead of the decode pyramid cache and the feasibility of combining it with PagedAttention-style systems. Extending the scoring theory: since LSE was shown superior to mean and mean+variance approximations, explore more accurate aggregation rules that resolve the mismatch in GQA group scoring (source: Appendix A). In short, PISA is a clean study showing that making selection cheaper is exactly what makes long context more practical. The next step is to verify whether this log-linear selection keeps its promise at production-scale LLMs and in serving systems.
