title: VC-Attention: Value Smoothing and Softmax Casting for Low-bit Attention

content:
Paper ActionPiece: Rethinking Action Tokenization Beyond Reconstruction Error, via Physical Ranking TL;DR — In autoregressive VLA (vision-language-action) models, the action tokenizer is the key interface that compresses continuous robot commands into discrete tokens and then reconstructs predicted tokens back into executable commands. Existing tokenizers only reduce pointwise reconstruction error such as MSE; they do not check whether the “fine adjustments” between demonstrations survive compression. This paper newly defines PRC (Physical Rank Consistency), which measures the degree to which the ranking of physical distances is preserved in the reconstructed action space, and proposes ActionPiece, which supervises representation learning and quantization jointly to preserve that relation. Under the same Qwen3-VL-4B policy training setup, it achieves state-of-the-art results of 94.8% on LIBERO and 68.8% on unseen LIBERO-Plus (source: Abstract, Table 1).
Key IdeaThe action tokenizer simultaneously determines the “prediction target” for policy learning and the “decoder” at execution time (source: §1). Prior work improved compression efficiency through coordinate discretization (RT-2, OpenVLA), frequency-domain compression (FAST), and learned vector quantization (FASTer, OAT, ActionCodec, X-Tokenizer) (source: §2.2), but did not sufficiently address the fact that compression itself changes the actions the robot ultimately executes (source: §1).
ActionPiece’s core insight boils down to three points.
MSE only reduces the error of individual actions; it does not coordinate the “direction” of reconstruction error across demonstrations (source: §3.1). After compression, similar actions cluster around a representative motion, but the adjustments needed for different contexts can be weakened, distorted, or inverted (source: §1, §3.1). Therefore, in addition to pointwise accuracy, one must evaluate preservation of the ranking of physical distances (PRC) and directly supervise that ranking itself as a training objective. The authors call this perspective “relational fidelity,” and to achieve it they apply rank supervision to both the representation learning stage and the codeword assignment stage (source: §1, Fig. 1).
Background: The Problem They SolvedThe “adjustments” the tokenizer silently erasesAcross demonstrations of the same task, repeated motions appear with subtle differences. For example, in “pick up the red can and put it in the box,” the grasp position varies slightly depending on object position, robot state, and execution stage (source: §3.1). In tasks requiring precise alignment, grasping, and contact, these small differences determine success or failure (source: §1, §3.1).
The tokenizer compresses these demonstrations into a discrete representation of finite capacity and then reconstructs them back into executable commands. This lossy compression inevitably produces reconstruction error $e_i = \hat x_i - x_i$. The reconstructed difference between two demonstration chunks $x_i$, $x_j$ decomposes as follows (source: Eq. 1):
$$ \hat x_j - \hat x_i = (x_j - x_i) + (e_j - e_i) $$The first term is the “action change” that actually exists in the demonstrations, and the second is the “extra change” that tokenization inserts. The problem is that MSE only reduces the magnitude of this second term and does not control its direction. As a result, the extra term can attenuate or amplify the original difference and can even flip its direction (source: §3.1).
Crucially, this distortion does not disappear even when the policy predicts the tokens “exactly.” Even if the VLA correctly reproduces the token sequence encoding a demonstration action, the decoder will still execute the “reconstructed version” of that action (source: §1, §3.1).
The landscape of existing approachesThe authors organize existing action interfaces into three branches (source: §2.1).
Discrete autoregressive: RT-2/OpenVLA discretize coordinates into bins, and FAST compresses action chunks into short token sequences. The advantage is that they can reuse the next-token prediction objective of a pretrained VLM as is (source: §2.1). Continuous prediction: OpenVLA-OFT ($\ell_1$ regression) and the RDT/$\pi_0$/GR00T family (diffusion, flow matching) directly predict real-valued action chunks (source: §2.1). Hybrid: $\pi_{0.5}$, HybridVLA, Fast-in-Slow, etc. mix discrete supervision with continuous execution (source: §2.1). Among the learned vector quantization family are FASTer (residual vector quantization + structural patching), OAT (nested dropout + coarse-to-fine alignment), ActionCodec (token budget, alignment, residual grammar), and X-Tokenizer (semantic supervision from a vision-language teacher) (source: §2.2). All of these focused on compression, ordering, and multimodal alignment, but none had a mechanism to measure or supervise “how compression changes the relations between demonstrations” (source: §2.2).
New Approach: ActionPiecePRC: Looking at “distance ranking,” not “distance values”The authors evaluate relation preservation through the relative ordering of physical distances. First they define the physical distance $d_{\text{phys}}$. This expresses the difference between two end-effector commands $a=(p, R, g)$ (position, rotation, gripper) as a weighted sum of normalized components (source: §4.2, Eq. 5):
$$ \delta_{\text{phys}}(a, a') = \alpha_p \left\|\frac{p - p'}{s_p}\right\|_2^2 + \alpha_R \left(\frac{d_{\text{SO(3)}}(R, R')}{s_R}\right)^2 + \alpha_g\,|g - g'|^2 $$The rotation distance is measured as the shortest geodesic angle on $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ (source: Eq. 4):
$$ d_{\text{SO(3)}}(R, R') = \left\|\mathrm{Log}(R^\top R')^{\vee}\right\|_2 $$The scales $s_p, s_R$ are fit to the training actions, and the group weights $\alpha_p, \alpha_R, \alpha_g$ are fixed within an embodiment (source: §4.2). The chunk-level distance averages the per-timestep distances.
Based on this distance, PRC@k measures, for each anchor $A_i$, how well the distance ranking to the $k$ nearest neighbors $N_i^k$ in the original action space agrees with the ranking to the same neighbors of the reconstruction $\hat A_i$, using the Spearman correlation $\rho_S$ ($k=32$) (source: §3.2, Eq. 2):
$$ \text{PRC@}k = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \rho_S\Big(\big[d_{\text{phys}}(A_i, A_j)\big]_{j\in N_i^k},\ \big[d_{\text{phys}}(\hat A_i, \hat A_j)\big]_{j\in N_i^k}\Big) $$The key design choice is that the ranking is measured in the decoded action space. This lets tokenizers be compared on the same physical basis regardless of token vocabulary, sequence length, or decoder architecture (source: §3.2). In short, MSE handles the fidelity of individual reconstructions, and PRC handles preservation of the physical distance ranking.
Two physical rank lossesActionPiece consists of a shallow Transformer encoder/decoder and residual vector quantization (RVQ). An action chunk $A\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times D}$ with $H$ steps is turned by the encoder $E_\phi$ into $S$ latent slots, and an RVQ of depth $Q$ and codebook size $K$ represents each slot as a sum of $Q$ codewords $q_s = \sum_{r=1}^{Q} e^{(r)}[z_s^{(r)}]$ (source: §4.1, Eq. 3). The total number of tokens is $T = SQ$. The decoder $D_\omega$ reconstructs the entire chunk at once from these $T$ tokens.
In addition to the reconstruction loss, the authors add two rank supervisions.
① PRP (Physical Rank Preservation) — After LayerNorm and unit $\ell_2$ normalization of the encoder features $\bar h_{i,s}$ and the selected codeword features $\bar e_{i,s}$ respectively, the slot-mean squared distances $d^2_{\text{enc}}$, $d^2_{\text{quant}}$ are computed and mixed $0.25:0.75$ to form the representation distance (source: §4.3, Eq. 6–7):
$$ d^2_{\text{rep}}(i,j) = 0.25\, d^2_{\text{enc}}(i,j) + 0.75\, d^2_{\text{quant}}(i,j) $$Then, for each anchor, the remaining actions in the batch are sorted by physical distance, and the near action at the 5th percentile ($q_{0.05}$) is selected as the positive (near) $j_i^+$, while the far action at the 95th percentile ($q_{0.95}$) is selected as the negative (far) $j_i^-$ (source: §4.3, Appx. B.3). The ranking loss imposes the near–far order (source: Eq. 8):
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_i \mathrm{softplus}\big(D_{ij_i^+} - D_{ij_i^-} + m_r\big),\quad m_r = 0.1 $$② QR (Quantization Regularization) — Rather than the representation distance, it imposes the same order on the mean Jensen–Shannon divergence between the codeword assignment probability distributions $\pi_{i,s}$ of each slot (source: §4.4, Eq. 9–10):
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{quant}} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_i \mathrm{softplus}\big(d_{\text{JS}}(i, j_i^+) - d_{\text{JS}}(i, j_i^-) + m_q\big),\quad m_q = 0.1 $$The two losses target two different stages of compression. PRP aligns the geometry of learned features to the physical order, and QR aligns the assignment into the discrete vocabulary (source: §4.4). The overall objective is as follows (source: §4.5, Eq. 12):
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{tok}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} + \lambda_{vq}\mathcal{L}_{\text{commit}} + \lambda_r \mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}} + \lambda_q \mathcal{L}_{\text{quant}} $$The weights are $\lambda_{vq}=0.25$ and $\lambda_r=\lambda_q=6.25\times10^{-4}$ (source: §4.5, Table 6). After training, the tokenizer is frozen; the encoder and quantizer supply the policy’s discrete targets, and the frozen decoder turns predicted tokens back into execution chunks. The VLA is trained only with standard next-token prediction $\mathcal{L}_{\text{VLA}} = -\sum_t \log p_\theta(z_t | I, \ell, z_{\lt t})$ (source: §4.5, Eq. 13).
flowchart TD A["Select anchor / near / far from demonstrations<br/>(based on physical distance d_phys)"] --> T["ActionPiece tokenizer"] T --> E["Encoder: 8-step chunk → 16 slots"] E --> Q["RVQ: 1 codeword per slot<br/>codebook size 512"] Q --> D["Decoder: 16 tokens → 8-step action reconstruction"] E --> P["PRP: d_rep(anchor,near) < d_rep(anchor,far)"] Q --> R["QR: JS(anchor,near) < JS(anchor,far)"] D --> M["MSE reconstruction loss"] How It Works: A Concrete ExampleTo aid understanding, let us give an illustrative example (we note that this is not an actual experimental result from the paper).
Suppose we have three action chunks in the “pick up the red can and put it in the box” task.
Chunk Gripper x position Role Anchor $A$ $x=0.00$ m Reference motion Near $n$ $x=+0.01$ m Context-dependent fine adjustment Far $f$ $x=+0.10$ m An entirely different grasp position The original physical distances are $d_{\text{phys}}(A,n)=0.01$ (small) and $d_{\text{phys}}(A,f)=0.10$ (large), so the ranking is $n < f$. This ranking must be preserved for the meaning of “fine adjustment” to survive.
Suppose that a tokenizer trained with MSE alone reconstructs them, yielding distances as follows (illustrative numbers).
Reconstruction comparison Original $d_{\text{phys}}$ After reconstruction $d_{\text{phys}}$ Ranking $\hat A$ vs $\hat n$ 0.01 0.08 — $\hat A$ vs $\hat f$ 0.10 0.05 — After reconstruction, $d(\hat A,\hat f) < d(\hat A,\hat n)$, so the ranking is flipped. The individual reconstruction errors were small, but the direction of those errors collapsed the boundary between “fine adjustment” and “entirely different motion” (source: consistent with the interpretation of Eq. 1 in §3.1). ActionPiece’s PRP and QR enforce this $n < f$ ranking in both the representation distance and the codeword assignment, training so that the ranking is preserved after reconstruction.
The quantitative evidence the paper presents is the correlation analysis in Fig. 2. Across 55 tokenizer-benchmark evaluations, PRC showed a Spearman correlation of $\rho_S = 0.681$ with policy success, while reconstruction fidelity (MSE ranking) showed $\rho_S = 0.544$ (source: Fig. 2, §5.2). In other words, “how well the distance ranking is preserved” is more strongly associated with downstream success than “how similar the distance values are”, which is the empirical basis for this design.
Performance Validation: Key ResultsSummary of experimental setupFour benchmarks cover three kinds of action data sources and different generalization conditions (source: §5.1).
LIBERO: In-distribution baseline. Simulated teleoperation demonstrations (20 Hz sampling). LIBERO-Plus: Evaluates a LIBERO-trained policy under 7 kinds of unseen perturbations (camera, robot, language, lighting, background, noise, layout). SimplerEnv: Real-to-sim transfer of a WidowX policy trained on BridgeData V2 real-robot demonstrations (5 Hz). VLA-Arena: Train on L0 (keyboard teleoperation, 10 Hz) and evaluate on L0–L2. The tokenizer is trained with AdamW, lr $1\times10^{-4}$, batch 128, for 100K steps, and the policy is trained with the StarVLA protocol on 8×NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs using AdamW (lr $1\times10^{-5}$, cosine schedule) + DeepSpeed ZeRO-2 (source: §5.1). In all comparisons, the backbone, prompt, optimizer, batch, training budget, 8-step prediction/execution horizon, seed, and evaluation protocol are held fixed (source: §5.1).
Matched comparison: LIBERO / LIBERO-PlusTable 1 compares results while changing only the action tokenizer on the same Qwen3-VL-4B policy (source: Table 1).
Tokenizer LIBERO (overall) LIBERO-Plus (overall) OAT 86.1 60.7 Standard RVQ 90.9 60.4 FASTerVQ* 91.3 62.6 FAST 92.1 64.3 ActionCodec 93.7 64.2 ActionPiece (Ours) 94.8 68.8 ActionPiece leads the strongest baseline (ActionCodec 93.7%) by +1.1p on LIBERO and the strongest baseline (64.3%) by +4.5p on unseen LIBERO-Plus (source: §5.3, Table 1). It ranks first in 6 of the 7 perturbation categories of LIBERO-Plus, supporting the claim that preserving adjustments at the execution stage is more advantageous when going outside the training distribution (source: §5.3).
Transfer evaluation: SimplerEnv / VLA-ArenaOn SimplerEnv (WidowX), ActionPiece achieved 71.9% on average, the best among the 15 compared models. It placed first on block stacking (58.3%), which requires precise placement, and was also strong on spoon (83.3%) and branch (91.7%) (source: §5.4, Table 2). This shows that physical relation supervision is also effective for tokenizers trained on real robot actions.
On VLA-Arena, the L0/L1/L2 success rates were 82.2% / 42.7% / 29.5%, with a 33-cell equal-weighted average of 51.5%, the best among the compared models (source: §5.4, Table 3). Despite training only on L0, it led the L1 and L2 averages by +7.0p and +5.0p respectively, and showed an advantage in L2 performance on static obstacles, dynamic obstacles, and unseen objects (source: §5.4).
Component ablation: The role of the two lossesTable 4 and Table 5 decompose the effect by removing each of the two physical rank losses (source: §5.5, Table 4–5).
Variant MSE($\times10^4$, ↓) PRC(↑) LIBERO(↑) LIBERO-Plus(↑) Standard RVQ 4.06 0.902 90.9 60.4 + PRP 3.63 0.947 93.8 65.4 + QR 3.92 0.916 92.9 62.4 ActionPiece (PRP + QR) 3.32 0.953 94.8 68.8 Three observations emerge. First, PRP contributes more individually (+PRP gives +5.0p on LIBERO-Plus). Second, adding QR raises LIBERO-Plus by a further +3.4p, so the two losses are complementary. Third, improvements in policy success move together with improvements in PRC (0.902→0.953) (source: §5.5). In particular, on camera perturbation, PRP alone jumps from 35.5% to 45.1% when combined, and the combination beats the individual losses in 6 perturbation categories (source: §5.5).
Appendix A also provides comparisons with alternative objectives. SIGReg, Neighborhood (pulling nearby actions together), and Temporal (matching temporal changes) can also raise policy success, but Neighborhood actually lowers PRC (0.889). ActionPiece simultaneously achieves the lowest MSE, the highest PRC, and the highest success rate on both benchmarks among them (source: Appx. A, Table 5).
Our Perspective: Strengths, Limitations, and Why This Work MattersStrengths The problem definition is sharp. The fact that “the tokenizer changes the executed action” has long been known in robotics, but this work elevates it into a measurable framework called “relational fidelity.” PRC is a clear contribution in that it lets tokenizers with different vocabularies, sequences, and decoders be compared on a single common physical basis (source: §3.2). The placement of supervision is convincing. The design that supervises the representation distance (PRP) and the codeword probabilities (QR) separately corresponds to the two stages of compression, “feature learning” and “discrete assignment,” and is conceptually clean and justified by ablations (source: §4.4, §5.5). The experiments are rigorous. In the matched comparison, everything from backbone and data to prompt, budget, and seed is held fixed, and the coverage spans in-distribution (LIBERO), out-of-distribution (LIBERO-Plus), real-to-sim (SimplerEnv), and difficulty generalization (VLA-Arena) (source: §5.1). LimitationsWe first cover the limitations the authors acknowledge or reveal.
For RVQ depth, $Q=1$ and $Q=2$ give similar downstream performance, so $Q=1$ was chosen as the final configuration. This means the depth benefit of residual quantization is limited on this task (source: Appx. B.2). The group weights $\alpha_p,\alpha_R,\alpha_g$ of the physical distance and the scales are fixed within an embodiment, and their specific values are not reported in the paper (source: §4.2, “not reported in the original”). Behind the overall advantage, there is per-task variance. For example, there are cases where it is not first, such as “place carrot on plate” (54.2%) on SimplerEnv or some categories on VLA-Arena (source: Table 2, Table 3). The potential limitations inferred from a reviewer’s perspective are as follows.
$\lambda_r=\lambda_q=6.25\times10^{-4}$ is a very small value, yet there is no sensitivity analysis for these weights (source: Table 6). The balance between losses may be sensitive to the data distribution. The effect on results of PRC’s hyperparameters ($k=32$, Spearman correlation) and the near/far percentiles (5%, 95%) was not ablated (source: §3.2, Appx. B.3). Table 1 compares tokenizers, whereas Tables 2 and 3 compare against full policies such as $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, and GR00T. There is no comparable apple-to-apple point of comparison that directly bridges these two kinds of comparisons with different conditions (source: Table 1 vs Table 2–3). Although SimplerEnv trained on real-robot demonstrations is real-to-sim, physical real-robot deployment performance is not reported (source: §5.4). Total computation (FLOPs/PF-days) and energy cost are not reported (“not reported in the original”). Why this work mattersAs long as VLA keeps the framework of “predicting discrete tokens,” the tokenizer is the bottleneck that sets the policy’s ceiling. ActionPiece redefines this bottleneck from the perspective of “preserving relations between actions” rather than “reconstructing individual actions,” and showed that this perspective actually yields gains in out-of-distribution generalization (source: §5.3, §6). The result that merely fixing the tokenizer yields a +4.5p (LIBERO-Plus) improvement in transfer performance under the same policy suggests that “representation design” is still an underexplored lever in robotics foundation models.
What’s Next?: The Road AheadThe paper does not list explicit future research directions, but one can propose paths that naturally follow from the results and limitations.
Revisiting multi-stage RVQ ($Q>1$). It is worth checking whether the current result that $Q=1$ and $Q=2$ are similar still holds once physical rank supervision is added (source: Appx. B.2). Generalizing the physical distance weights. Learning $\alpha_p,\alpha_R,\alpha_g$ adaptively from the task or data, rather than fixing them per embodiment, is key to extending this method to various robot morphologies (source: §4.2). Making PRC a standard diagnostic metric. PRC can be used as an independent quality metric for choosing a tokenizer. If reporting PRC alongside MSE when selecting a tokenizer becomes standard practice, the impact of this paper could exceed that of ActionPiece itself (source: the correlation analysis in Fig. 2). Combining with continuous and diffusion policies. PRP/QR is supervision for discrete tokenizers, but the principle of “preserving the direction of adjustments between demonstrations” is a general principle transplantable to flow/diffusion policies of the $\pi_0$ family and to hybrid designs (source: connected to the hybrid discussion in §2.1). Paper DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: A Multimodal MoE That Cuts the KV Cache to 1/4 While Raising Performance FurtherTL;DR. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, released by DeepSeek-AI, is a multimodal MoE with a 552B backbone that supports up to a 1M token context. It combines Causal Encoder-Decoder (CED), Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2), FP4 KV cache, and SWA Bounded Replay to cut the global KV cache to 890 bytes per token (about 1/4 of the predecessor DeepSeek-V4-Flash) and the persistent KV cache to about 1/8 (source: Abstract, §6). Even so, it stands shoulder to shoulder with closed frontier models on agent benchmarks, including DeepSWE v1.1 74.2% and Terminal-Bench 2.1 90.6% (source: Table 3, §5.3.2).
Key IdeaThe central hypothesis of this paper can be summarized as follows. The authors hypothesize that by using [a CED structure that projects the decoder’s global KV from the encoder output + CSA2’s cross-layer KV/index reuse + FP4 cache precision + SWA Bounded Replay], they can overcome [the compute, storage, and bandwidth bottlenecks of long-context serving] and achieve [better performance with 1/4–1/8 of the predecessor’s KV cache].
The key point is that it “does not tighten just one axis but tightens three axes at once.” The KV cache cost shrinks as the product of (1) entry size (the axis that reduces KV heads/dimensions, as in GQA·MLA), (2) sequence dimension (the axis that compresses $m$ tokens into a single entry, as in CSA·HCA), and (3) layer dimension (cross-layer cache reuse) (source: §2.3). Prior work touched only some of these axes — IndexCache reused Top-K indices, YOIO shared routing, and HySparse reused the KV of dense layers, but none covered all three axes (source: §2.3). What sets DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash apart is that it exploits all three axes simultaneously, and further combines them with FP4 precision and a deployment strategy (SWA Bounded Replay) to push compression to its limit.
Background: The Problem They SolvedWith the spread of long-running agents, model workloads are increasingly becoming input-heavy. This simultaneously explodes three costs (source: Abstract, §1):
Compute: prefill is expensive. As an agent repeats tool calls, cache misses become more frequent, and each time a new prompt must be prefilled again (source: §2.2). Storage: global KV pressures HBM capacity, and persistent KV pressures SSD/host memory capacity (source: §1). Bandwidth: cache migration and loading become bottlenecks on I/O and interconnect bandwidth (source: §1). DeepSeek-V4 already greatly reduced compute cost with a combination of global attention (full context) + local Sliding-Window Attention (SWA). But the problem was that “storage” remained. SWA’s KV is bounded by the window size, but the global KV keeps growing in proportion to the sequence length, so for sufficiently long sequences the global KV comes to occupy most of the runtime KV footprint (source: §1). In other words, compute was solved, and now storage and data movement have emerged as the new bottleneck. The authors frame this as “KV cache management has become a foundational capability for deployment” (source: §1).
The state of SOTA at this point can be summarized as follows. Long-context compute was largely resolved by sparse attention (DeepSeek-AI 2025, 2026b), but on the persistent storage, reuse, and transfer side, HBM/SSD capacity and bandwidth were still the limiting factors (source: §1, §3.2.1). And the comparison targets at the time of publication are open frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3, and closed models such as Opus-5 and GPT-5.6 (source: Table 3).
New Approach: CED + CSA2 + SWA Bounded ReplayLet’s look at the overall architecture first. The language backbone has 40 causal Transformer layers, with the bottom 20 as a causal encoder and the top 20 as a decoder. The first 2 layers use only SWA, and the rest use CSA2. On top of this are attached a vision encoder (DeepSeek-ViT), Engram (conditional memory), and DSpark (speculative decoding for inference acceleration) (source: §2.1, Fig. 3).
flowchart TB subgraph CED["Causal Encoder-Decoder (40 layers)"] direction TB IN["Text + Image Embeddings"] VE["DeepSeek-ViT (32L) + MLP Projector"] ENC["Encoder (20 layers)<br/>L1-2: SWA only<br/>L3-20: CSA2 (m=2)"] HID["Encoder final hidden state H_L/2"] DEC["Decoder (20 layers)<br/>CSA2 (m=1)"] OUT["Output (autoregressive)"] end IN --> VE VE --> ENC ENC --> HID HID -- "project W_KV^l, W_Z^l (eq.1)" --> DEC DEC --> OUT How this architecture addresses each of the three core costs is the essence of this paper.
1) CED: Halving PrefillCED extends the idea of YOCO. In a traditional Transformer, every layer builds its KV from its own hidden state. In CED, the decoder’s global KV is built not from its own hidden state but from the last encoder layer’s hidden state $H_{L/2}$ via per-layer projection weights $W_{KV}^{l}$ (source: §2.2, eq. 1):
$$C_l = H_{L/2} W_{KV}^{l},\quad Z_l = H_{L/2} W_{Z}^{l},\quad l > \frac{L}{2}$$Therefore, at prefill time, running only the bottom half ($L/2$) yields the top half’s global KV almost for free. SWA is left as-is per layer, in order to preserve the computational depth of local KV generation. As a result, when the sequence length $N \gg n_{win}$, the prefill complexity is halved from $O(NL)$ to $O(NL/2 + n_{win}\times L/2) \approx O(NL/2)$ (source: §2.2).
Effect: active parameters are split into 8B at prefill and 16B at decode. This is an advantageous structure for input-heavy agent workloads (source: Abstract, §2.1).
2) CSA2: Tightening Even the Layer DimensionCSA2 is a sparse attention that simplifies and extends DeepSeek-V4’s CSA, statically assigning one of three modes to each layer (source: §2.3.1, Fig. 4). What they have in common is that every mode directly computes its own query and SWA KV. The difference lies in where the global main KV, indexer K, and Top-K indices come from:
Mode Main KV Indexer K Top-K indices Work performed Full Compute directly Project from main KV Generate anew Full path (indexer + sparse attention) Reindex Reuse previous layer Reuse Rescore with own indexer Q → new selection Recompute indexer only Reuse Reuse previous layer (unnecessary) Reuse as-is Sparse attention only (no indexer) Two simplifications were added. CSA used overlap between adjacent compressed entries and absolute positional embeddings at compression ratio $m$, but CSA2 removed these, and indexer K is likewise obtained by projecting the main KV instead of a separate compression path. This simplifies the implementation and improves training efficiency (source: §2.3).
They also introduced a Hierarchical Sparse Indexer exclusively for the decoder. By having a deep indexer share the candidate pool selected by a shallow indexer, the per-query scoring cost of the deep indexer is changed from “linear in context length” to “constant.” The first Full layer scans everything to create a candidate pool of 2,048 blocks × 8 positions = up to 16,384 candidates, and subsequent Reindex layers pick 512 within that pool (source: §2.3.2, §4.2.1, Fig. 5). This restriction is introduced at post-training time so that training and inference use the same retrieval domain (source: §2.3.2).
3) FP4 main KV + SWA Bounded Replay: Tightening Storage FP4 KV cache: main KV was lowered from FP8 to FP4 (E2M1, one E4M3 scale per 16 channels), cutting storage to nearly half. The accuracy loss is reported to be “marginal” (source: §2.4.4). SWA KV is kept at FP8 because of quantization sensitivity (source: §2.4.4). SWA Bounded Replay: SWA KV is not persistently stored on SSD; instead, when needed, only the most recent $n_{win}$ (=128) tokens are replayed to approximately reconstruct it. Exact reconstruction requires a full forward pass over $L\times n_{win}$ tokens, but experiments confirmed that this “approximation” causes almost no performance degradation (source: §1, §3.2.2). This newly establishes a storage-compute trade-off. Decomposing how these three axes multiply to produce the final numbers (source: §3.2.1, §2.4.4):
Target Reduction factor Mechanism Global KV (HBM) about 1/4 CSA2 cross-layer reuse (~1/2) × FP4 cache (~1/2) → 890 bytes per token Persistent KV (SSD/host) about 1/8 SWA KV removal (~1/2) × global KV compression (1/4) The authors also describe this as reductions of 437× (vs. V1) and 4× (vs. V4-Flash) (source: Fig. 1b).
Auxiliary Extensions: Single-Pass mHC, Engram, DSpark Single-Pass mHC: the previous mHC’s 3-kernel implementation was fused into a single kernel (Mega-mHC), cutting activation memory traffic by half. The key trick is to shift the input mixing coefficients by one block to remove the dependency (source: §2.4.1, eq. 6). The performance degradation is “negligible” (source: §2.4.1). Engram: a conditional memory module that separates memorization from computation, splitting 196B parameters across two modules (layers 1, 14). It stores N-gram orders {2,3,4}, 8 hash heads, and per-head tables of about 16M entries in FP8 (source: §2.4.2). DSpark: speculative decoding with semi-autoregressive drafting + confidence-scheduled verification. It is trained separately with the backbone frozen, and is also trained together during post-training (source: §2.4.3). How It Works: A Concrete ExampleLet’s understand CSA2’s three modes with a toy example. (This is an illustrative example, not an experimental result from the paper.)
Suppose 6 layers form one group. The paper’s actual layout divides the encoder’s 18 layers into 3 groups of 6, with only the first layer of each group as Full and the remaining 5 as Reuse (source: §4.2.1). The 20 decoder layers are divided into 5 groups of 4, with only the first group as Full+3Reuse and the remaining 4 groups as Reindex+3Reuse (source: §4.2.1).
Suppose the context has 8 tokens $[t_1,\dots,t_8]$, and for simplicity “select Top-2” (in reality Top-512, source: §4.2.1).
Layer 1 (Full): build the main KV for all 8 tokens, and the indexer scores them to pick Top-2 (e.g., $t_3, t_7$). This KV and index are stored as “the most recent Full result.” Layer 2 (Reuse): build only its own query, and perform only sparse attention using Layer 1’s main KV + Top-2 ($t_3,t_7$) as-is. Since the indexer is not run at all, both compute and cache are saved. Layer 3 (Reuse): likewise reused. Here layers 2 and 3 do not store the main KV redundantly, so the cache shrinks. Conversely, in Reindex mode (the decoder’s remaining groups), Layer 2 reuses the KV but rescoring with its own indexer Q can change the Top-2 to $t_2,t_5$ — that is, it becomes possible to “have each layer differ in which tokens it attends to while sharing storage” (source: §2.3.1).
Let’s also sketch CED’s prefill flow briefly (source: §2.2):
sequenceDiagram participant P as Prompt (N tokens) participant E as Encoder (L/2 layers) participant D as Decoder (L/2 layers) P->>E: full forward (compute global KV) E->>D: project H_{L/2} → decoder global KV (eq.1) Note over D: SWA replays only recent n_win tokens<br/>(Decoder SWA Bounded Replay) D->>D: decode begins Because the decoder’s global KV comes from the encoder’s last hidden state, prefill essentially ends at the encoder. What remains is the decoder’s SWA KV, and even this is handled by “replaying only the most recent $n_{win}$ tokens” (source: §2.2, §3.2.2). So, as Fig. 2 shows, even when the single-token decode FLOPs grows from a 4K to a 1M context (256×), it increases by only 1/4 — a markedly flatter curve than DeepSeek-V4-Flash (source: Fig. 2).
Performance Validation: Main ResultsBase model (Table 1). DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-Base (552B, active 8B/16B) achieves performance equal to or better than its predecessor V4-Pro-Base (1.6T, active 49B) with 1/3 the total parameters and 1/4 the active parameters (source: §4.3.2, Table 1). It leads on MMLU-Pro 74.1 (vs Pro 73.5), HumanEval 79.4 (vs 76.8), GSM8K 93.0 (vs 92.6), BigCodeBench 60.6 (vs 59.2), and reports a 5–10% improvement on held-out evaluation (source: §1, Table 1). That said, there are items where it lags Pro, such as LongBench-V2 (45.2 vs 51.5) and SimpleQA (42.3 vs 55.2), so “excellent relative to its compactness” is more accurate than “dominant across all fields” (source: Table 1).
Post-training (Table 3). Agent performance stands out in particular:
Benchmark V4.1-Flash Best competitor Notes Codeforces (Rating) 3471 V4-Pro 3348 Its own best MathArena Apex 65.6% Kimi-K3 65.6% Tied for 1st GPQA Diamond 90.9% GPT-5.6 94.1% Improved over V4-Flash 89.9% DeepSWE v1.1 74.2% Opus-5 74.0% +19.8pt over V4-Flash 54.4% Terminal-Bench 2.1 90.6% Opus-5 89.1% 1st Automation-Bench 54.8% Opus-5 50.3% 1st Terminal-Bench 3.0 30.0% Opus-5 43.3% Gap exists Terminal-Bench 4.0 31.2% Opus-5 51.8% Gap exists (All numbers sourced from Table 3, §5.3.2. The DeepSWE +19.8pt is calculated from 54.4→74.2.)
The key point is DeepSWE v1.1 74.2%, a jump of +19.8pt from the predecessor’s 54.4%, edging out Opus-5 (74.0%), and also beating the strongest closed model on Terminal-Bench 2.1 90.6%, Automation-Bench 54.8%, and Agents’ Last Exam 31.8% (source: §5.3.2). In cybersecurity it also set open-source SOTA on CyberGym at 88.1% (source: §5.3.2).
Reasoning Effort knob. Interestingly, this is a training technique that controls the amount of reasoning with a scalar $b\in\{1,\dots,100\}$. In RL, the token-length penalty coefficient is decreased exponentially with effort as $k(b)=k_0\exp(-(b-b_{min})/\tau)$, allowing longer thinking at higher effort (source: §5.1.4, eq. 10). As a result, raising effort from 25→100 increases the average Pass@1 over 8 reasoning benchmarks from 67.1%→76.3%, DeepSWE from 66.0%→74.2%, and Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 82.4%→90.6%, but uses about 2.5× more tokens (source: §5.3.2, Fig. 9). The gains are concentrated in the front, so the 60–80 range recovers the accuracy of the maximum setting with less than half the tokens (source: §5.3.2). The production API exposes three tiers: max=100, high=75, low=50 (source: Table 2).
Multi-agent (Fig. 10). Superior at all deadlines versus single-agent. ProgramBench Almost@1 goes from multi 13.59% (@1h)→30.04% (@8h peak) vs single 12.79%→20.39%, and FrontierSWE v2 Mean@5 goes from multi 13.50%→32.90% (@20h) vs single 10.50%→28.20% (source: §5.3.5).
Our View: Strengths, Limitations, and Why This Research MattersStrengths. (1) The biggest contribution is that it was the first to complete the triple-product structure of compression in one model. It tightens the three axes of layer, sequence, and entry size simultaneously, and bundles precision (FP4) and deployment (SWA Bounded Replay) into that as well (source: §2.3). (2) SWA Bounded Replay, which “gives up storage and buys it back with compute,” is a practical insight — starting from the observation that SWA KV’s access pattern does not fit the long-term retention policy of a persistent cache, it turns a catastrophic miss into “a cheap and elegant degradation” (source: §3.2.1). (3) The asymmetric activation of prefill 8B / decode 16B is a design that meshes precisely with the input-heavy agent era (source: §2.2).
Limitations. Let’s distinguish the limitations the authors explicitly acknowledge from potential limitations from a reviewer’s perspective.
Limitations acknowledged by the authors (source: §6):
CSA2’s selection error and SWA Bounded Replay’s approximate state reconstruction can cause performance degradation on untested extreme inputs. A finite test suite cannot cover all boundary conditions. A science-oriented agent (requiring specialized domain knowledge, such as Terminal-Bench 4.0) still has a gap versus gigantic models. Due to benchmark saturation, one should not mistake “similar score = equivalent capability,” and there is still a difference from the frontier on the hardest reasoning and edge cases. Potential limitations the reviewer reads out:
Long-term dependency of approximate reconstruction: SWA Bounded Replay relies on the assumption of “replaying only the most recent $n_{win}$ tokens.” The possibility that the state becomes inaccurate at the cache resumption boundary was mentioned by the authors, but long-term empirical evidence on whether this error accumulates over long multi-turn sessions is still lacking (source: §3.2.2, §6). Imbalance in performance: in the base model, SimpleQA, LongBench-V2, MGSM, etc. lag V4-Pro (source: Table 1). “Excellent relative to its compactness” and “absolute superiority” should be read as distinct. Asymmetry in reproducibility/openness: checkpoints were released (Abstract), but most evaluations are based on in-house harnesses, in-house scaffolds, and in-house data pipelines (§4.3.2, §5.1.1), making it difficult for outsiders to reproduce under identical conditions. Why this research matters. Ultimately, the message of this paper is that “intelligence and efficiency are not separate things.” If a small footprint of 8B–16B active parameters can handle most of the daily tasks of closed frontier models (the authors claim over 95%) (source: §1), the cost barrier for long-term agent deployment drops substantially. More than the simple number of cutting the KV cache to 1/4, the shift in perspective — “reformulating storage, compute, and bandwidth as a single optimization problem” — carries greater implications for follow-up research.
What’s Next?: The Road AheadThe directions the authors propose are (1) simultaneous scaling of architecture, pretraining, and post-training, (2) model-harness co-design, and (3) expanding stress tests of the boundary conditions of sparse retrieval and SWA state reconstruction (source: §6).
Reasonable next steps a reviewer might add here:
Quantifying CSA2’s selection error: characterizing exactly which input distributions make sparse attention’s selection error fatal, using metrics such as recall@K, would yield an operational guide for “when it is safe to use this model.” Sub-FP4 precision: since main KV has been lowered to FP4, the next step is analyzing the causes of SWA KV’s sensitivity (currently kept at FP8 for sensitivity reasons) and selectively applying low precision to it (source: §2.4.4). Generalizing the Hierarchical Sparse Indexer: the candidate pool is used only in the decoder (§2.3.2), and the upper bound (performance) and lower bound (cost) trade-off of extending it to the encoder as well is an interesting research topic. Ultimately, this model is a new reference point for the goal of “long context, cheaply but intelligently.” The number 890 bytes/token has become another bar for the next generation to break.
